doi:10.1175/aies-d-25-0036.1.title: Using Large Language Models to Produce Literature Reviews: Usage Patterns of Microphysics Parameterizations in WRF Simulations from 2699 Publications
doi:10.1175/aies-d-25-0036.1.summary: Large language models (LLMs) afford opportunities for using computers for intensive tasks, providing research opportunities that have not been considered before. One such opportunity is a systematic interrogation of the scientific literature. Here, we show how an LLM assists in constructing a literature review, focusing on feasibility, process design, and resulting outcomes. We constructed a database of 2699 publications associated with precipitation simulations in the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) Model, with the goal of learning how microphysics parameterizations were used and reviewing forecast errors across a diverse array of precipitation simulations. The large language model GPT-4 Turbo was used to extract information about model configurations and performance from the text of 2699 publications identified using Web of Science and Scopus searches. Our results reveal the landscape of how nine of the most popular microphysics parameterizations have been used around the world: Lin, Ferrier, WRF single-moment 3-class, 5-class, 6-class, Goddard Cumulus Ensemble, Morrison, Thompson, and WRF double-moment. More studies used single-moment parameterizations before 2020 and double-moment parameterizations after 2020. Except for simulations using Lin, Ferrier, and Goddard that tended to underestimate precipitation over almost all locations, the remaining six parameterizations tended to overestimate precipitation, particularly over China, Southeast Asia, the western United States, and central Africa. This method could be used by other researchers to help understand how the increasingly massive body of scientific literature can be harnessed through the power of artificial intelligence to solve their research problems. Significance Statement Microphysics parameterization is used to represent unresolved cloud and precipitation processes and hydrometeor populations at subgrid scales in numerical weather prediction models. However, to our knowledge, no systematic literature review, meta-analysis, or other large study exists on the usage and performance of different microphysics parameterizations. This study used a large language model to analyze 2699 scientific publications associated with precipitation simulations in the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) Model. The most popular parameterization was the WRF single-moment 6-class microphysics scheme (WSM6) before 2020 but Thompson after 2020. Seven out of nine parameterizations tended to overestimate precipitation. Our results synthesize previous studies on microphysics parameterizations, summarizing their reported performance in precipitation simulations. Moreover, this study demonstrates a novel approach to solving scientific problems through the large-scale analysis of existing scientific publications.

doi:10.1175/aies-d-22-0055.1.title: Efficient Data-Driven Gap Filling of Satellite Image Time Series Using Deep Neural Networks with Partial Convolutions
doi:10.1175/aies-d-22-0055.1.summary: The abundance of gaps in satellite image time series often complicates the application of deep learning models such as convolutional neural networks for spatiotemporal modeling. Based on previous work in computer vision on image inpainting, this paper shows how three-dimensional spatiotemporal partial convolutions can be used as layers in neural networks to fill gaps in satellite image time series. To evaluate the approach, we apply a U-Net-like model on incomplete image time series of quasi-global carbon monoxide observations from the Sentinel-5 Precursor ( Sentinel-5P ) satellite. Prediction errors were comparable to two considered statistical approaches while computation times for predictions were up to three orders of magnitude faster, making the approach applicable to process large amounts of satellite data. Partial convolutions can be added as layers to other types of neural networks, making it relatively easy to integrate with existing deep learning models. However, the approach does not provide prediction uncertainties and further research is needed to understand and improve model transferability. The implementation of spatiotemporal partial convolutions and the U-Net-like model is available as open-source software. Significance Statement Gaps in satellite-based measurements of atmospheric variables can make the application of complex analysis methods such as deep learning approaches difficult. The purpose of this study is to present and evaluate a purely data-driven method to fill incomplete satellite image time series. The application on atmospheric carbon monoxide data suggests that the method can achieve prediction errors comparable to other approaches with much lower computation times. Results highlight that the method is promising for larger datasets but also that care must be taken to avoid extrapolation. Future studies may integrate the approach into more complex deep learning models for understanding spatiotemporal dynamics from incomplete data.

doi:10.1029/2019ms001725.title: Impact of a Multi‐Layer Snow Scheme on Near‐Surface Weather Forecasts
doi:10.1029/2019ms001725.summary: Snow cover properties have a large impact on the partitioning of surface energy fluxes and thereby on near‐surface weather parameters. Snow schemes of intermediate complexity have been widely used for hydrological and climate studies, whereas their impact on typical weather forecast time scales has received less attention. A new multilayer snow scheme is implemented in the European Centre for Medium‐range Weather Forecasts Integrated Forecasting System and its impact on snow and 2‐m temperature forecasts is evaluated. The new snow scheme is evaluated offline at well‐instrumented field sites and compared to the current single‐layer scheme. The new scheme largely improves the representation of snow depth for most of the sites considered, reducing the root‐mean‐square error averaged over all sites by more than 30%. The improvements are due to a better description of snow density in thick and cold snowpacks, but also due to an improved representation of sporadic melting episodes because of the inclusion of a thin top snow layer with a low thermal inertia. The evaluation of coupled 10‐day weather forecasts shows an improved representation of snow depth at all lead times, demonstrating a positive impact at the global scale. Regarding the impact on weather parameters, the multilayer snow scheme improves the simulated minimum 2‐m temperature, by decreasing the positive bias and improving the amplitude of the diurnal cycle over snow‐covered regions. However, the increased variability of the 2‐m temperature can have a detrimental impact in regions characterized by preexisting errors in the daily mean temperature, associated with errors in cloud processes or surface albedo.

doi:10.1002/jame.20018.title: A simplified PDF parameterization of subgrid‐scale clouds and turbulence for cloud‐resolving models
doi:10.1002/jame.20018.summary: Over the past decade a new type of global climate model (GCM) has emerged, which is known as a multiscale modeling framework (MMF). Colorado State University's MMF represents a coupling between the Community Atmosphere Model and the System for Atmospheric Modeling (SAM) to serve as the cloud‐resolving model (CRM) that replaces traditionally parameterized convection in GCMs. However, due to the high computational expense of the MMF, the grid size of the embedded CRM is typically limited to 4 km for long‐term climate simulations. With grid sizes this coarse, shallow convective processes and turbulence cannot be resolved and must still be parameterized within the context of the embedded CRM. This paper describes a computationally efficient closure that aims to better represent turbulence and shallow convective processes in coarse‐grid CRMs. The closure is based on the assumed probability density function (PDF) technique to serve as the subgrid‐scale (SGS) condensation scheme and turbulence closure that employs a diagnostic method to determine the needed input moments. This paper describes the scheme, as well as the formulation of the eddy length which is empirically determined from large eddy simulation (LES) data. CRM tests utilizing the closure yields good results when compared to LESs for two trade‐wind cumulus cases, a transition from stratocumulus to cumulus, and continental cumulus. This new closure improves the representation of clouds through the use of SGS condensation scheme and turbulence due to better representation of the buoyancy flux and dissipation rates. In addition, the scheme reduces the sensitivity of CRM simulations to horizontal grid spacing. The improvement when compared to the standard low‐order closure configuration of the SAM is especially striking.

doi:10.1029/2025ms005288.title: Evaluation of E3SM Simulated Aerosols and Aerosol‐Cloud Interactions Across GCM and Convection‐Permitting Scales
doi:10.1029/2025ms005288.summary: This paper introduces an Earth system modeling testbed for predicting aerosols and aerosol‐cloud interactions (ACIs) at convection‐permitting scales. Using the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM) version 2 with a four‐mode Modal Aerosol Module, we conduct simulations at 3.25 km resolution on a regionally refined mesh (RRM) across four regions with distinct aerosol and cloud regimes. Results are compared with the standard 100 km E3SM configuration and evaluated against satellite, aircraft, and ground‐based observations. We find that increasing model resolution improves heavy precipitation simulation but amplifies positive bias in light drizzle at coarse resolution. These resolution‐induced changes affect cloud and aerosol properties to varying degrees across regions. Generally, cloud cover and liquid water path (LWP) show better agreement with satellite retrievals at 3.25 km, though surface‐based comparisons suggest otherwise. Aerosol composition remains poorly represented at both resolutions. The RRM increases Aitken mode aerosol number concentrations via enhanced new particle formation. However, accumulation mode aerosols are decreased at higher resolution as aerosol removals become more efficient. This partially contributes to fewer cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) and lower cloud droplet number concentrations (), which produces larger model biases in some scenarios. These findings suggest that solely increasing horizontal resolution to kilometer scales is insufficient to broadly improve aerosol and cloud predictions without concurrent advancements in physical and chemical process representations. Nonetheless, the RRM moderately improves key ACI relationships such as CCN‐ correlation, reflecting enhanced aerosol activation representation. The LWP‐ relationship is also better captured by RRM, suggesting a better characterization of LWP adjustment.

doi:10.1029/2026gl125943.title: Weathering Flux Calculations From Climate Model Outputs Show a Decrease in Alkalinity Fluxes to the Ocean During the Last Deglaciation
doi:10.1029/2026gl125943.summary: Variations in chemical weathering rates during the last deglaciation remain poorly constrained, although some studies suggest little net change because climatic and sea‐level changes act in opposite directions. Here, we use climate model outputs to calculate weathering fluxes with empirical equations, estimating their impacts on the deglacial evolution of riverine alkalinity fluxes to the ocean. With our model ensemble, we obtain a decreasing trend of alkalinity fluxes, resulting from loess erosion and flooding shelves (whose effects are counteracting those of a climate getting warmer and wetter). Such a reduction in alkalinity source could affect the marine carbon cycle, contributing to the deglacial atmospheric increase. Our results also underline the need for further model development to reduce runoff biases and implement evolving coastlines in Earth System Models, as well as the importance of a good representation of lithological data.

doi:10.1029/2021gl094779.title: Double Intertropical Convergence Zones in Coupled Ocean‐Atmosphere Models: Progress in CMIP6
doi:10.1029/2021gl094779.summary: Reducing the double Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) bias has been the subject of intensive research in the climate modeling community. Recent studies have shown small to little progress in the ensemble of Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) models compared to Phase 3 (CMIP3) and Phase 5 (CMIP5) models in simulating the ITCZ. This study distinguishes the performances of the ensemble of CMIP models and the sub‐ensemble of top five models in reference to the double ITCZ bias by using the spatial correlation as the metric. We show that while there was little progress in the whole CMIP6 ensemble, there is progress in the top five models from CMIP5 to CMIP6. These models have largely eliminated the bias. This improvement is masked in the whole ensemble by the larger inter‐model spread. Results point to promising directions to which coupled models are heading to eradicate the chronic double ITCZ bias.

doi:10.1029/2020ef001778.title: Increased Flood Exposure Due to Climate Change and Population Growth in the United States
doi:10.1029/2020ef001778.summary: Precipitation extremes are increasing globally due to anthropogenic climate change. However, there remains uncertainty regarding impacts upon flood occurrence and subsequent population exposure. Here, we quantify changes in population exposure to flood hazard across the contiguous United States. We combine simulations from a climate model large ensemble and a high‐resolution hydrodynamic flood model—allowing us to directly assess changes across a wide range of extreme precipitation magnitudes and accumulation timescales. We report a mean increase in the 100‐year precipitation event of ~20% (magnitude) and >200% (frequency) in a high warming scenario, yielding a ~30–127% increase in population exposure. We further find a nonlinear increase for the most intense precipitation events—suggesting accelerating societal impacts from historically rare or unprecedented precipitation events in the 21st century.

doi:10.1029/2026ea005073.title: An Enhanced Hydrometeor Detection Algorithm for Precipitation Identification in GPM
doi:10.1029/2026ea005073.summary: Precipitation is a fundamental component of the climate system, linking the water and energy cycles and regulating climate variability, feedbacks, and extremes. Accurate precipitation detection provides essential constraints on the global water cycles and serves as a key benchmark for evaluating climate model performance. The Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission, equipped with the first spaceborne dual‐frequency radar (DPR), offers unprecedented capability for observing the three‐dimensional structure of global precipitation, including phase, intensity and microphysical properties. However, existing precipitation detection algorithm does not explicitly account for weak radar signals, limiting their ability to capture the early development and full evolution of precipitation systems. In this study, we propose an enhanced hydrometeor detection algorithm for GPM DPR observations that combines a bilateral filter technique and a power‐probability weighting scheme. Through effectively suppressing background noise while preserving physically meaningful weak signals, our method can significantly improve the detection of small hydrometeors at high altitudes and along precipitation boundaries—regions that are frequently missed by the current GPM operational algorithm. Validation using collocated CloudSat observations demonstrates substantial improvements of our method, with increases of 63.6% the Ka band and a 37.5% in the Ku band. These advancements provide a more comprehensive depiction of precipitation systems structure and offer improved observational support for enhancing precipitation estimation and climate modeling.

doi:10.1029/2020jd033990.title: Evaluating the Relationship Between Lightning and the Large‐Scale Environment and its Use for Lightning Prediction in Global Climate Models
doi:10.1029/2020jd033990.summary: The objective of this study is to determine the relationship between lightning observed by the Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM) Lightning Imaging Sensor (LIS) and seven large‐scale environmental variables obtained from the 3‐hourly Modern‐Era Retrospective analysis for Research and Application version 2 (MERRA‐2) reanalysis in the tropics and subtropics. The large‐scale environmental variables used are: convective available potential energy (CAPE), normalized CAPE (nCAPE), lifting condensation level (LCL), column saturation fraction (r), 700‐hPa omega, low‐level wind shear (LS) from 900 to 700 hPa, and deep wind shear (DS) from 900 to 300 hPa. All environmental variables show a significant shift toward larger values when lightning is present except for shear. DS decreases when lightning is present, while LS shows little mean change. However, strong geographical differences exist in the relationship between the environmental variables and lightning occurrence, particularly between land and ocean and the tropics and subtropics. Using a logistic regression, a lightning parameterization for global climate models (GCMs) is created using the above environmental variables as predictors while also adding geographic indicators (coast, slope, and latitude) and terms representing interactions between the predictors. The logistic regression predicts lightning occurrence accurately up to 86% of the time and is further applied to MERRA‐2. While there are regions of overprediction and underprediction, the lightning parameterization performance shows promising potential for use in GCMs.

doi:10.1038/s41612-024-00579-4.title: Global increase in future compound heat stress-heavy precipitation hazards and associated socio-ecosystem risks
doi:10.1038/s41612-024-00579-4.summary: Compound extremes of lethal heat stress-heavy precipitation events (CHPEs) seriously threaten social and ecological sustainability, while their evolution and effects at the global scale under climate warming remain unclear. Here we develop the global picture of projected changes in CHPEs under various scenarios and investigate their socioeconomic and ecosystem risks combining hazard, exposure, and vulnerability through the composite indicator approach. We find a high percentage of heat stress is followed by heavy precipitation, probably driven by atmospheric conditions. Global average frequency and intensity of CHPEs are projected to increase in the future under high-emission scenarios. Joint return periods of CHPEs are projected to decrease globally, predominantly driven by changes in heat stress extremes. In the long-term future, over half of the population, gross domestic product, and gross primary productivity may face high risk in most regions, with developed regions facing the highest risks under SSP5-8.5 and developing regions facing the highest risks under SSP3-7.0.

doi:10.5194/wcd-1-277-2020.title: Northern Hemisphere blocking simulation in current climate models: evaluating progress from the Climate Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 to 6 and sensitivity to resolution
doi:10.5194/wcd-1-277-2020.summary: Global climate models (GCMs) are known to suffer from biases in the simulation of atmospheric blocking, and this study provides an assessment of how blocking is represented by the latest generation of GCMs. It is evaluated (i) how historical CMIP6 (Climate Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6) simulations perform compared to CMIP5 simulations and (ii) how horizontal model resolution affects the simulation of blocking in the CMIP6-HighResMIP (PRIMAVERA – PRocess-based climate sIMulation: AdVances in high-resolution modelling and European climate Risk Assessment) model ensemble, which is designed to address this type of question. Two blocking indices are used to evaluate the simulated mean blocking frequency and blocking persistence for the Euro-Atlantic and Pacific regions in winter and summer against the corresponding estimates from atmospheric reanalysis data. There is robust evidence that CMIP6 models simulate blocking frequency and persistence better than CMIP5 models in the Atlantic and Pacific and during winter and summer. This improvement is sizeable so that, for example, winter blocking frequency in the median CMIP5 model in a large Euro-Atlantic domain is underestimated by 33 % using the absolute geopotential height (AGP) blocking index, whereas the same number is 18 % for the median CMIP6 model. As for the sensitivity of simulated blocking to resolution, it is found that the resolution increase, from typically 100 to 20 km grid spacing, in most of the PRIMAVERA models, which are not re-tuned at the higher resolutions, benefits the mean blocking frequency in the Atlantic in winter and summer and in the Pacific in summer. Simulated blocking persistence, however, is not seen to improve with resolution. Our results are consistent with previous studies suggesting that resolution is one of a number of interacting factors necessary for an adequate simulation of blocking in GCMs. The improvements reported in this study hold promise for further reductions in blocking biases as model development continues.

doi:10.1175/mwr-d-21-0245.1.title: GEFSv12 Reforecast Dataset for Supporting Subseasonal and Hydrometeorological Applications
doi:10.1175/mwr-d-21-0245.1.summary: For the newly implemented Global Ensemble Forecast System, version 12 (GEFSv12), a 31-yr (1989–2019) ensemble reforecast dataset has been generated at the National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP). The reforecast system is based on NCEP’s Global Forecast System, version 15.1, and GEFSv12, which uses the Finite Volume 3 dynamical core. The resolution of the forecast system is ∼25 km with 64 vertical hybrid levels. The Climate Forecast System (CFS) reanalysis and GEFSv12 reanalysis serve as initial conditions for the Phase 1 (1989–99) and Phase 2 (2000–19) reforecasts, respectively. The perturbations were produced using breeding vectors and ensemble transforms with a rescaling technique for Phase 1 and ensemble Kalman filter 6-h forecasts for Phase 2. The reforecasts were initialized at 0000 (0300) UTC once per day out to 16 days with 5 ensemble members for Phase 1 (Phase 2), except on Wednesdays when the integrations were extended to 35 days with 11 members. The reforecast dataset was produced on NOAA’s Weather and Climate Operational Supercomputing System at NCEP. This study summarizes the configuration and dataset of the GEFSv12 reforecast and presents some preliminary evaluations of 500-hPa geopotential height, tropical storm track, precipitation, 2-m temperature, and MJO forecasts. The results were also compared with GEFSv10 or GEFS Subseasonal Experiment reforecasts. In addition to supporting calibration and validation for the National Water Center, NCEP Climate Prediction Center, and other National Weather Service stakeholders, this high-resolution subseasonal dataset also serves as a useful tool for the broader research community in different applications.

doi:10.1175/waf-d-21-0130.1.title: The High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR): An Hourly Updating Convection-Allowing Forecast Model. Part II: Forecast Performance
doi:10.1175/waf-d-21-0130.1.summary: The High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) is a convection-allowing implementation of the Advanced Research version of the Weather Research and Forecast (WRF-ARW) Model that covers the conterminous United States and Alaska and runs hourly (for CONUS; every 3 h for Alaska) in real time at the National Centers for Environmental Prediction. The high-resolution forecasts support a variety of user applications including aviation, renewable energy, and prediction of many forms of severe weather. In this second of two articles, forecast performance is documented for a wide variety of forecast variables and across HRRR versions. HRRR performance varies across geographical domain, season, and time of day depending on both prevalence of particular meteorological phenomena and the availability of both conventional and nonconventional observations. Station-based verification of surface weather forecasts (2-m temperature and dewpoint temperature, 10-m winds, visibility, and cloud ceiling) highlights the ability of the HRRR to represent daily planetary boundary layer evolution and the development of convective and stratiform cloud systems, while gridded verification of simulated composite radar reflectivity and quantitative precipitation forecasts reveals HRRR predictive skill for summer and winter precipitation systems. Significant improvements in performance for specific forecast problems are documented for the upgrade versions of the HRRR (HRRRv2, v3, and v4) implemented in 2016, 2018, and 2020, respectively. Development of the HRRR model data assimilation and physics paves the way for future progress with operational convective-scale modeling. Significance Statement NOAA’s operational hourly updating convection-allowing model, the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR), is a key tool for short-range weather forecasting and situational awareness. Improvements in assimilation of weather observations, as well as in physics parameterizations, has led to improvements in simulated radar reflectivity and quantitative precipitation forecasts since the initial implementation of HRRR in September 2014. Other targeted development has focused on improved representation of the diurnal cycle of the planetary boundary layer, resulting in improved near-surface temperature and humidity forecasts. Additional physics and data assimilation changes have led to improved treatment of the development and erosion of low-level clouds, including subgrid-scale clouds. The final version of HRRR features storm-scale ensemble data assimilation and explicit prediction of wildfire smoke plumes.

doi:10.1175/2009waf2222252.1.title: Toward Better Understanding of the Contiguous Rain Area (CRA) Method for Spatial Forecast Verification
doi:10.1175/2009waf2222252.1.summary: The contiguous rain area (CRA) method for spatial forecast verification is a features-based approach that evaluates the properties of forecast rain systems, namely, their location, size, intensity, and finescale pattern. It is one of many recently developed spatial verification approaches that are being evaluated as part of a Spatial Forecast Verification Methods Intercomparison Project. To better understand the strengths and weaknesses of the CRA method, it has been tested here on a set of idealized geometric and perturbed forecasts with known errors, as well as nine precipitation forecasts from three high-resolution numerical weather prediction models. The CRA method was able to identify the known errors for the geometric forecasts, but only after a modification was introduced to allow nonoverlapping forecast and observed features to be matched. For the perturbed cases in which a radar rain field was spatially translated and amplified to simulate forecast errors, the CRA method also reproduced the known errors except when a high-intensity threshold was used to define the CRA (≥10 mm h−1) and a large translation error was imposed (>200 km). The decomposition of total error into displacement, volume, and pattern components reflected the source of the error almost all of the time when a mean squared error formulation was used, but not necessarily when a correlation-based formulation was used. When applied to real forecasts, the CRA method gave similar results when either best-fit criteria, minimization of the mean squared error, or maximization of the correlation coefficient, was chosen for matching forecast and observed features. The diagnosed displacement error was somewhat sensitive to the choice of search distance. Of the many diagnostics produced by this method, the errors in the mean and peak rain rate between the forecast and observed features showed the best correspondence with subjective evaluations of the forecasts, while the spatial correlation coefficient (after matching) did not reflect the subjective judgments.

doi:10.1175/waf-d-17-0023.1.title: Performance of the New NCEP Global Ensemble Forecast System in a Parallel Experiment
doi:10.1175/waf-d-17-0023.1.summary: A new version of the Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS, v11) is tested and compared with the operational version (v10) in a 2-yr parallel run. The breeding-based scheme with ensemble transformation and rescaling (ETR) used in the operational GEFS is replaced by the ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) to generate initial ensemble perturbations. The global medium-range forecast model and the Global Forecast System (GFS) analysis used as the initial conditions are upgraded to the GFS 2015 implementation version. The horizontal resolution of GEFS increases from Eulerian T254 (~52 km) for the first 8 days of the forecast and T190 (~70 km) for the second 8 days to semi-Lagrangian T574 (~34 km) and T382 (~52 km), respectively. The sigma pressure hybrid vertical layers increase from 42 to 64 levels. The verification of geopotential height, temperature, and wind fields at selected levels shows that the new GEFS significantly outperforms the operational GEFS up to days 8–10 except for an increased warm bias over land in the extratropics. It is also found that the parallel system has better reliability in the short-range probability forecasts of precipitation during warm seasons, but no clear improvement in cold seasons. There is a significant degradation of TC track forecasts at days 6–7 during the 2012–14 TC seasons over the Atlantic and eastern Pacific. This degradation is most likely a sampling issue from a low number of TCs during these three TC seasons. The results for an extended verification period (2011–14) and the recent two hurricane seasons (2015 and 2016) are generally positive. The new GEFS became operational at NCEP on 2 December 2015.

arxiv:2611.05592.title: Distinguishing Initial-Condition and Model Error Using Machine-Learning Weather Models
arxiv:2611.05592.summary: Differentiable weather models allow atmospheric initial conditions to be directly optimized to shadow a known trajectory, which we take from a reanalysis dataset. Here, we extend this optimization to include the forecast model, GraphCast, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA). We compare model optimization with initial-condition (IC) optimization, and then joint optimization, where both are tuned simultaneously. When compared against a control forecast initialized with reanalysis data, LoRA and IC optimization individually produce similar improvements. We find similar results when IC and LoRA are jointly optimized across a spectrum of solutions where a tuning coefficient smoothly shifts the weight of the joint optimization from all-LoRA to all-IC; forecast improvement is not unique to the relative contributions of model and IC corrections. To better discriminate the source of error, we introduce a second model, Pangu-Weather, as a supervisor that gates IC updates during joint optimization. This gated optimization is the same as before, except that IC updates at each epoch are accepted only when they improve the forecasts of both models; otherwise, only the LoRA update is accepted. Results show that this cross-model constraint substantially improves agreement between the two models in their response to the same optimized ICs, narrowing the gap in mean forecast error reduction from 64% to 10%. Moreover, when used together, the LoRA and IC corrections from the gated optimization yield GraphCast forecast improvements similar to those from the ungated optimization. These results imply that model error that is encoded in the ungated ICs is shifted to the LoRA corrections via gating, yielding IC corrections that may provide better analysis estimates.

arxiv:2610.35693.title: GNN-VIEW: Visual Inspection and Explanation of Graph-based Earth-System Models
arxiv:2610.35693.summary: Machine learning Earth-system models are becoming increasingly important, and so is their development. Graph-based models, one of the most prominent approaches, allow developers to constrain the learning process before training via graph connectivity. Yet, developing these models remains challenging: the graph is built algorithmically with little intuition about the final result beyond static plotting, which requires extra work and is often not detailed enough. Even after successful training, how the model arrives at forecasts remains obscure. We present GNN-VIEW, an interactive browser-based tool that supports the development of such systems. GNN-VIEW exposes the graph's information pathways, allowing model developers to debug the graph structure before training. After training, GNN-VIEW uses attribution-based explainability to reveal which input features are used by the trained model for a given forecast. This helps developers understand why a model fails. We showcase the usefulness of GNN-VIEW in the construction stage of a graph for an ocean forecasting model, and in explaining poorly predicted precipitation of a trained weather forecasting model during Hurricane Laura.

arxiv:2610.24627.title: UDL-RT: A unified differentiable all-sky microwave radiative transfer model with learnable parameterizations
arxiv:2610.24627.summary: Radiance-based retrievals and data assimilation require radiative transfer models (RTMs) to simulate radiances and quantify their sensitivities to atmospheric and surface conditions. Conventional RTMs often rely on separately maintained forward, tangent-linear, and adjoint codes, complicating model development and extension. Here, we present the Unified Differentiable and Learnable Radiative Transfer model (UDL-RT), a PyTorch-based framework for all-sky microwave radiative transfer that couples neural-network (NN) parameterizations of gaseous absorption, hydrometeor bulk scattering properties (BSPs), and ocean surface emissivity with an explicit radiative transfer solver in a unified differentiable computational graph. Automatic differentiation directly computes Jacobians with respect to input variables, reducing the model maintenance burden. The NN parameterizations offer flexible representations of complex nonlinear relationships. For example, the NN gas-absorption parameterization reduces the standard deviation of brightness-temperature (TB) errors by approximately 60-85% in the water-vapour channels compared with linear regression. Moreover, UDL-RT propagates loss gradients to trainable parameters to optimize physical parameterizations against observations, with GPU-accelerated batched computation supporting efficient iterative learning. Using Microwave Humidity Sounder-2 (MWHS-2) observations, we optimize the snow BSP parameterization through gradient-based learning. The optimized parameterization improves agreement between simulated and observed TB distributions and reduces the systematic bias and skewness of observation-minus-background (O-B) departures. Overall, UDL-RT integrates radiance simulation, sensitivity analysis, and parameterization optimization within a unified framework, supporting future remote sensing retrieval and data assimilation applications.

arxiv:2609.23732.title: Predicting low-latitude ionospheric Total Electron Content (TEC) over the Indian sector under variable space weather conditions using solar wind parameters
arxiv:2609.23732.summary: Accurate prediction of ionospheric Total Electron Content (TEC) during geomagnetically disturbed conditions remains challenging, particularly when empirical models perform poorly during storms and neural network (NN) approaches rely explicitly on geomagnetic indices such as Kp/Ap or Dst/SYM-H. In this study, we develop an NN-based model to predict TEC variations over the Indian longitude sector without incorporating geomagnetic indices as inputs. The model is trained on the full-year (2024) Global Ionospheric Map (GIM) TEC dataset at a 15-minute cadence, together with solar wind parameters: Interplanetary Magnetic Field (IMF) $B_z$, velocity ($V_{sw}$), and density ($N_p$), along with the F10.7 cm solar radio flux. Seasonal and diurnal variability are represented using sinusoidal transformations of Day of Year (DOY) and hour of day (HOD). An optimized architecture with 96 hidden neurons yields strong training performance ($R^2$ $\sim$ 0.96, RMSE $\sim$ 5.4, and MAE $\sim$ 3.8 TECU). Independent predictions for the year 2025 demonstrate robust generalization under both quiet and geomagnetically active conditions. Quiet-time residuals are generally confined within $\pm$10 TECU, while during moderate and strong storm-time conditions, the model maintains comparable error bounds across most of the Indian region, despite not being trained on geomagnetic indices. The results indicate that solar wind parameters, combined with the F10.7 solar flux and cyclical temporal encoding, contain sufficient information to reproduce geomagnetic storm-time TEC variability. This study therefore demonstrates the applicability of the proposed approach for regional TEC prediction and ionospheric nowcasting, with potential applications in GNSS positioning, satellite navigation, radio communication systems, and the future development of operational ionospheric forecasting tools.

doi:10.5194/gmd-9-1747-2016.title: ESMValTool (v1.0) – a community diagnostic and performance metrics tool for routine evaluation of Earth system models in CMIP
doi:10.5194/gmd-9-1747-2016.summary: A community diagnostics and performance metrics tool for the evaluation of Earth system models (ESMs) has been developed that allows for routine comparison of single or multiple models, either against predecessor versions or against observations. The priority of the effort so far has been to target specific scientific themes focusing on selected essential climate variables (ECVs), a range of known systematic biases common to ESMs, such as coupled tropical climate variability, monsoons, Southern Ocean processes, continental dry biases, and soil hydrology–climate interactions, as well as atmospheric CO2 budgets, tropospheric and stratospheric ozone, and tropospheric aerosols. The tool is being developed in such a way that additional analyses can easily be added. A set of standard namelists for each scientific topic reproduces specific sets of diagnostics or performance metrics that have demonstrated their importance in ESM evaluation in the peer-reviewed literature. The Earth System Model Evaluation Tool (ESMValTool) is a community effort open to both users and developers encouraging open exchange of diagnostic source code and evaluation results from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP) ensemble. This will facilitate and improve ESM evaluation beyond the state-of-the-art and aims at supporting such activities within CMIP and at individual modelling centres. Ultimately, we envisage running the ESMValTool alongside the Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF) as part of a more routine evaluation of CMIP model simulations while utilizing observations available in standard formats (obs4MIPs) or provided by the user.

doi:10.1029/2017ms001217.title: A Higher‐resolution Version of the Max Planck Institute Earth System Model (MPI‐ESM1.2‐HR)
doi:10.1029/2017ms001217.summary: The MPI‐ESM1.2 is the latest version of the Max Planck Institute Earth System Model and is the baseline for the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 and current seasonal and decadal climate predictions. This paper evaluates a coupled higher‐resolution version (MPI‐ESM1.2‐HR) in comparison with its lower‐resolved version (MPI‐ESM1.2‐LR). We focus on basic oceanic and atmospheric mean states and selected modes of variability, the El Niño/Southern Oscillation and the North Atlantic Oscillation. The increase in atmospheric resolution in MPI‐ESM1.2‐HR reduces the biases of upper‐level zonal wind and atmospheric jet stream position in the northern extratropics. This results in a decrease of the storm track bias over the northern North Atlantic, for both winter and summer season. The blocking frequency over the European region is improved in summer, and North Atlantic Oscillation and related storm track variations improve in winter. Stable Atlantic meridional overturning circulations are found with magnitudes of ~16 Sv for MPI‐ESM1.2‐HR and ~20 Sv for MPI‐ESM1.2‐LR at 26°N. A strong sea surface temperature bias of ~5°C along with a too zonal North Atlantic current is present in both versions. The sea surface temperature bias in the eastern tropical Atlantic is reduced by ~1°C due to higher‐resolved orography in MPI‐ESM‐HR, and the region of the cold‐tongue bias is reduced in the tropical Pacific. MPI‐ESM1.2‐HR has a well‐balanced radiation budget and its climate sensitivity is explicitly tuned to 3 K. Although the obtained reductions in long‐standing biases are modest, the improvements in atmospheric dynamics make this model well suited for prediction and impact studies.

doi:10.1002/advs.78271.title: Improved Skills for Predicting Sub‐Seasonal to Seasonal Global Sea Surface Temperature
doi:10.1002/advs.78271.summary: Accurate prediction of global sea surface temperature at sub‐seasonal to seasonal (S2S) timescales is critical for drought and flood forecasting, as well as for improving disaster preparedness in human society. Operational physics‐based numerical models are run to predict S2S sea surface temperature and corresponding climate indices, such as El Niño‐Southern Oscillation. However, these models are hampered by computational inefficiencies, rapidly dissipating ocean‐atmosphere initial conditions, and significant uncertainty and biases. Here, we introduce a novel spatiotemporal deep learning neural network to model the nonlinear and complex coupled atmosphere‐ocean weather systems. This model, named as CAS‐Canglong, incorporates climatic and temporal features and employs a self‐attention mechanism to enhance the prediction of global S2S sea surface temperature pattern. Compared to the physics‐based models, it shows higher computational efficiency and more predictive capability, improving one to three months sea surface temperature predictive skill by 55.6 ± 14.1% to 63.4 ± 15.5% in six ocean regions with dominant influence on S2S variability over land. This achievement underscores the huge potential of deep learning for largely improving forecasting skills at the S2S timescales over land.

doi:10.1007/s10707-026-00601-2.title: Self-supervised, physics-constrained super-resolution for wind mapping in the absence of high-resolution training references: a case study in Brazil
doi:10.1007/s10707-026-00601-2.summary: Planning renewable-energy expansion at the national scale requires wind maps far more detailed than sparse meteorological networks and coarse reanalysis grids can typically offer. This study introduces PC-SRCNN, a physics-constrained, self-supervised super-resolution framework that lifts ERA5 wind fields over Brazil from a native 0.25° grid to 0.025°, folding in soft regularization terms for horizontal kinematic consistency and the logarithmic vertical wind profile. The model was evaluated against observations from 190 meteorological stations from Brazil’s INMET network across all twelve months of 2024, benchmarked against IDW, Kriging, U-Net, SRCNN, and a variant constrained only by horizontal kinematics (PC-SRCNN𝜑). The full PC-SRCNN was the only model to outperform native ERA5 with statistical significance in every month, cutting MAE by 5.6–11.0%, reaching vertical-profile R² between 0.80 and 0.87, and posting the lowest error at 133 of the 190 stations (70.0%); the PC-SRCNN𝜑 variant, in contrast, performed significantly worse than ERA5, and the purely data-driven models failed to consistently beat it. These findings show that physical regularization aids wind-field super-resolution only when it respects the vertical structure of the atmospheric boundary layer, suggesting the potential of this framework as a computationally lightweight approach for super-resolution wind mapping in settings where conventional numerical downscaling is computationally demanding. Self-supervised PC-SRCNN framework enhances ERA5 from 0.25° to 0.025° over Brazil. Evaluated against 190 INMET stations throughout all of 2024. PC-SRCNN reduces MAE by 5.6% to 11.0% versus ERA5 in every month. Isolated kinematic regularization (PC-SRCNN𝜑) degrades performance versus ERA5. PC-SRCNN has the lowest error at 133 of 190 stations (70.0%) nationwide.

doi:10.15666/aeer/2404_87838810.title: A HYBRID DEEP LEARNING FRAMEWORK FOR LONG-TERM RUNOFF FORECASTING: INTEGRATING TIME SERIES MODELING AND MACHINE LEARNING
doi:10.15666/aeer/2404_87838810.summary: Long-term runoff forecasting is essential for sustainable water resource management, flood mitigation, and climate adaptation. However, existing hydrological and deep learning models often struggle to simultaneously capture multi-scale temporal dependencies, non-stationarity, and spatial heterogeneity in runoff processes. To address these challenges, this study proposes a Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Long-Term Runoff Forecasting (HDF-LRF), integrating Climate-Aware Temporal Decomposition (CATD), Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM), Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT), and XGBoost ensemble learning. The framework was developed using globally representative datasets, including GRDC, GRUN, and ERA5, covering 7,841 hydrological stations across diverse climatic regions. CATD was employed to separate trend, seasonal, and residual runoff components, while BiLSTM and TFT captured short- and long-term temporal dependencies. XGBoost was used to combine model outputs and enhance predictive performance. Experimental results demonstrate that HDF-LRF achieved an NSE of 0.918, RMSE of 18.4 mm/month, KGE of 0.903, and R² of 0.941, outperforming conventional hydrological, statistical, and deep learning baselines. Cross-regional transfer experiments showed a generalization ratio of 0.960, indicating strong robustness across hydroclimatic regions. The proposed framework provides an accurate, interpretable, and scalable solution for long-term runoff forecasting under current and future climate conditions.

doi:10.1029/2025wr041874.title: Big Data for Small Streams: Leveraging a Coarse National Model to Enhance Fine‐Resolution Stream Temperature Predictions
doi:10.1029/2025wr041874.summary: Predictive stream temperature models are commonly used to address spatial and temporal gaps in observational data because stream temperature information is essential for environmental management decisions. National models capture broad patterns driven by climate, topography, and seasonality, but often lack the spatial resolution to simulate fine‐scale variation in groundwater discharge, riparian shading, or tributary inflows. In contrast, watershed models may simulate finer‐resolution patterns but miss regional drivers or be limited by scarcity of observations. To generate watershed‐extent, fine‐resolution stream temperature predictions, we developed 18 multiscale machine‐learning models that leverage (a) a broad‐extent, coarse‐resolution stream temperature model and (b) finer‐resolution observations and predictor data. The coarse‐resolution model simulates daily stream temperature across the conterminous United States on the National Hydrologic Geospatial Fabric (13.7 km median reach length; 865,364 km total). The fine‐resolution models simulate daily stream temperature on the National Hydrography Dataset Plus version 2 (1.5 km median; 5,192,808 km total). We compared multiscale models to seven purely broad‐ (national) or watershed‐extent models, testing them in eight watersheds (436–985 km2) with differing hydrologic settings and under realistic data availability scenarios. Especially when observations within a watershed were scarce, multiscale models generated more accurate predictions than national or watershed‐specific models. A recurrent graph convolution neural network pretrained on coarse predictions and fine‐tuned on watershed‐specific observations was most accurate across watersheds and data scenarios. These results highlight that leveraging both coarse, national results and watershed‐specific data can increase model accuracies, particularly when observations within a watershed are spatially or temporally limited.

doi:10.26877/lpt.v5i3.1087.title: Identification of Atmospheric Dynamics of a Tropical Hail Event and Application of Radar Reflectivity Nowcasting Using a UNet-ConvLSTM2D Deep Learning Model
doi:10.26877/lpt.v5i3.1087.summary: Hail is a small-scale hydrometeorological phenomenon threatening disaster-prone regions of Indonesia, yet understanding of its atmospheric dynamics and deep learning-based radar nowcasting remain limited. This study characterizes the atmospheric conditions of the Depok City hailstorm on 28 October 2024 and evaluates a hybrid UNet-ConvLSTM2D model in predicting radar reflectivity. The study employed Column Maximum (CMAX) radar reflectivity data in PNG and VOL formats from the Soekarno-Hatta Class I Meteorological Station, cloud-top temperature and Cloud Convective Overlay data from Himawari-9 satellite imagery, and ERA5 reanalysis data on storm thermodynamic and kinematic conditions, while radar data from January 2023 to October 2024 were used for model training and validation. Model performance was assessed using Mean Squared Error (MSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), Critical Success Index (CSI), and Heidke Skill Score (HSS) across five reflectivity thresholds. Results show maximum radar reflectivity exceeding 55 dBZ at 08.18 UTC and 08.42 UTC, cloud-top temperatures of approximately -61°C to -73°C, and Convective Available Potential Energy (CAPE) of 524-590 J/kg with weak vertical wind shear of 2.4-2.8 m/s from ERA5, confirming a moderately unstable tropical convective environment. Prediction results yielded average values of 184.5897 for MSE, 9.7081 for MAE, and 0.3956 for SSIM, with CSI decreasing from 0.588 to 0.284 and HSS from 0.637 to 0.057 as lead time increased from 8 to 56 minutes. These findings are expected to enhance understanding of the atmospheric dynamics contributing to hail and support wider deep learning-based nowcasting for early warning in tropical Indonesia.

doi:10.3390/app162211462.title: LightRCAN: A Lightweight Super-Resolution Method for ERA5 Temperature Fields with Cross-Pressure-Level Transferability
doi:10.3390/app162211462.summary: Temperature data are fundamental to meteorological and climatological research. High-Resolution (HR) fields are essential for regional climate, model validation, and extreme weather assessment. This study proposes a Lightweight Residual Channel Attention Network (LightRCAN) for spatial super-resolution (SR) reconstruction of ERA5 temperature fields, which is the fifth-generation global atmospheric reanalysis produced by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). We reduce the resolution 0.25° ERA5 to 0.5°, create HR and Low-Resolution (LR) data pairs via bicubic interpolation, and train the network to reconstruct HR spatial structures from LR inputs. Results show LightRCAN accurately recovers spatial details. Compared with bicubic and bilinear interpolation, LightRCAN achieves lower reconstruction errors. Compared with the Residual Channel Attention Network (RCAN), LightRCAN reduces the number of parameters by 85% and floating-point operations (FLOPs) by 83%, while incurring only a 0.16 dB drop in Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), thereby achieving a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off. We also evaluate cross-pressure-level transferability by freezing the backbone and fine-tuning the upsampling module and the reconstruction convolutional layer (3.6% of parameters). This strategy achieves the best balance between reconstruction performance and parameter efficiency, outperforming direct transfer. LightRCAN offers a computationally efficient solution for reconstruction.

doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0362741.title: DTCN-RevIN: A Densely Temporal Causal Network with reversible instance normalization for enhanced weather forecasting via multi-scale feature integration
doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0362741.summary: Accurate weather forecasting is of paramount importance for disaster prevention, agriculture, and resource management, yet traditional Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) systems such as the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model face inherent limitations in temporal resolution and computational efficiency when capturing rapidly evolving atmospheric dynamics. Meanwhile, existing deep learning approaches—including Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN), and Transformers—struggle with long-range temporal dependencies, distribution shift, and scalability. To address these challenges, this study proposes the Densely Temporal Causal Network with Reversible Instance Normalization (DTCN), a deep learning architecture that combines: (1) causal dilated convolutions for efficient temporal modeling, (2) dense inter-layer connections for enhanced feature propagation, (3) multi-scale feature integration, and critically, (4) RevIN standardization to address distribution shift in meteorological time series. Through 250 independent station-level model training runs (5 architectures × 10 stations × 5 random seeds), we systematically evaluate DTCN against four deep learning baseline architectures (TCN, LSTM, Transformer, and LSTM-Attention) for the 32→6 short-range forecasting configuration. Results show that: (i) DTCN achieves competitive top-tier overall performance, with RMSE of 0.0052 ± 0.0004 and R2 of 0.37 ± 0.06; (ii) DTCN matches TCN in rounded overall RMSE and R2, while showing slightly lower variance than TCN; (iii) all evaluated architectures achieve positive overall R2 with RevIN standardization (0.22–0.37); and (iv) per-variable results indicate variable-dependent advantages, with LSTM/LSTM-Attention performing best for temperature, TCN performing best for humidity, and DTCN remaining competitive across all three meteorological variables. These findings establish DTCN as a competitive data-driven alternative for short-range weather forecasting rather than an unambiguous winner across every metric and variable.

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-73361-6.title: A physics guided hybrid modeling framework for rainfall runoff forecasting in data scarce regions
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-73361-6.summary: Rainfall-runoff (R-R) forecasting in data-scarce regions remains challenging due to limited hydrometeorological observations, uncertainties in satellite-based precipitation products (SPPs), and the inability of individual modeling approaches to fully represent complex watershed dynamics. To address these challenges, this study develops a physics guided hybrid modeling framework that integrates bias-corrected satellite precipitation products, signal decomposition techniques, process-based hydrological modeling, and deep learning (DL) for improved runoff simulation and forecasting. In the proposed framework, physical knowledge is incorporated through the soil and water assessment tool (SWAT), which provides physically meaningful representations of watershed processes, while a long short-term memory (LSTM) network learns residual nonlinear relationships between physically simulated and observed runoff responses. Three widely used SPPs, including CHIRPS, IMERG, and PERSIANN-CDR, were evaluated against available rainfall observations, and a PDF-based additive bias correction approach was applied to improve precipitation estimates. Wavelet transform (WT) and variational mode decomposition (VMD) were further investigated within a time consistent feature construction framework to extract hydrologically relevant temporal patterns from corrected precipitation inputs and SWAT-simulated runoff outputs. The framework was evaluated in two hydroclimatically contrasting watersheds in Iran, namely the semi-arid Tabriz Basin and the humid Ghaem Shahr Basin. Results indicated that CHIRPS provided the most reliable precipitation estimates among the tested SPPs, while VMD outperformed WT in extracting temporal characteristics relevant to runoff generation. The proposed VMD-SWAT-LSTM framework generally achieved superior or comparable performance compared with standalone SWAT, LSTM, and conventional SWAT-LSTM models during training, validation, and testing periods under a temporally consistent evaluation framework. During the training phase, the proposed framework achieved CC = 0.99, NSE = 0.96, and RMSE = 2.61 m3.s− 1 in Tabriz Basin, and CC = 0.98, NSE = 0.97, and RMSE = 0.58 m3.s− 1 in the Ghaem Shahr Basin. The proposed approach also demonstrated improved robustness in multi-step-ahead forecasting (up to 7 days), although predictive performance decreased with increasing lead time, and maintained robust performance under uncertainty according to Monte Carlo (MC) analysis. The findings demonstrate that combining physically based watershed representation with decomposition assisted data-driven (DD) error learning within a physics-guided framework can improve R-R forecasting accuracy and robustness in data-scarce regions. The proposed methodology showed robust performance in the two investigated hydroclimatically contrasting basins, suggesting its potential for hydrological prediction in data-scarce regions. However, its transferability to other basins and broader hydrological and climatic conditions requires further evaluation.

doi:10.1007/s00704-026-06633-w.title: Early warning of meteorological drought in Morocco’s Atlas mountains: a multi-paradigm benchmark of satellite-augmented deep learning and tree-based models
doi:10.1007/s00704-026-06633-w.summary: Meteorological drought monitoring in Morocco’s High Atlas and Anti-Atlas Mountains remains reactive, yet few predictive studies have combined satellite observations with spatiotemporal deep learning in mountainous terrain. We develop a Convolutional Gated Recurrent Unit (ConvGRU) framework to forecast the 6-month Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI-6) across the High Atlas and Anti-Atlas at 1- to 3-month lead times. The model ingests 18 input channels combining CHIRPS precipitation, ERA5-Land reanalysis fields, satellite-derived NDVI, and static terrain features over a 115 × 210-pixel domain at 5.5 km resolution, with a strict leakage-free temporal split. At a 1-month lead, the ConvGRU and a non-spatial gradient-boosted ensemble (XGBoost) achieved nearly equal forecast accuracy (RMSE = 0.696 and 0.698, respectively), with the ConvGRU improving on damped persistence by 11.8% (Diebold-Mariano p = 0.003) and ridge regression by 9.7% (RMSE = 0.771). The added architectural complexity of spatiotemporal deep learning did not translate into superior forecast skill in this data regime, with the non-spatial gradient-boosted ensemble matching the convolutional models across horizons. In a test-period evaluation of the severe April 2024 drought (92% of the area affected), both the spatiotemporal and non-spatial models recovered most of the drought extent one month in advance (ConvGRU 81%, XGBoost 94%), far exceeding the 29% recovered by damped persistence. As the forecast horizon extends to two and three months, predictive skill across all architectures decays rapidly toward the baseline, defining a clear practical limit on meteorological drought predictability in this mountainous region. Together, these results show that while an operational one-month early warning window is achievable in this topographically complex region, adding spatiotemporal network complexity does not extend the predictability window beyond one month.

doi:10.1109/jstars.2026.3738080.title: Geo-ARD: A Hybrid ARDB-Guided Residual Diffusion Model for Geospatial Wind Field Super-Resolution
doi:10.1109/jstars.2026.3738080.summary: High-resolution (HR) ocean wind field data is undamental to meteorology and oceanography, yet satellite-derived products (e.g., OCN) are spatiotemporally sparse. Conversely, reanalysis data (e.g., ERA5) offers global, hourly coverage but at a coarse low-resolution (LR), suffering from systematic bias and an inability to resolve fine-scale structures. To bridge this data gap, we propose geospatial attention-based residual dense block (ARDB)-guided residual diffusion (Geo-ARD), a novel 5× super-resolution framework that generates high-fidelity 0.05$^\circ$ wind fields from 0.25$^\circ$ inputs. Our framework introduces a two-stage approach to systematically address both domain bias and resolution enhancement. First, a pretrained alignment network, optimized with a hybrid regression and contrastive loss, maps the biased LR ERA5 data into an aligned feature space consistent with HR OCN observations. Second, the core of our model is a guided diffusion process conditioned on a novel ARDB. This hybrid CNN–Transformer conditioner embeds efficient self-attention mechanisms directly within its dense blocks, enabling it to capture both the local textures and the critical long-range spatial dependencies inherent in global wind fields. The denoising diffusion model is then tasked with a simplified objective: generating only the high-frequency residual within an analytically defined latent space, allowing it to focus entirely on fine-detail synthesis. To optimize for high-impact events, the framework is trained with a compound loss, featuring a novel quadratically weighted L1 diffusion loss that prioritizes accuracy in high-energy (strong wind) regions, and a PatchGAN-based adversarial loss applied directly to the ARDBNet’s deterministic prior to enforce perceptual sharpness. Experiments against both general-purpose baselines and two domain-specific diffusion models show that Geo-ARD achieves the best values across all seven reported metrics. Relative to the strongest domain-specific baseline, CorrDiff, it reduces root mean squared error (RMSE) by 2.33% and Gradient mean absolute error by 57.89% on the temporally held-out test set. A geographically disjoint evaluation over the Indian Ocean further yields the best RMSE of 1.531 without target-region adaptation, supporting the cross-regional transferability of the proposed framework. Because Geo-ARD reconstructs scalar wind-speed magnitude rather than complete vector dynamics, these results are interpreted as evidence of numerical and structural fidelity to the OCN reference data, rather than verification of fluid-dynamical conservation or operational forecasting skill.

doi:10.5194/isprs-archives-l-4-w2-2026-1.title: AI-Based Framework for Urban Climate Downscaling: A Case Study of Sofia
doi:10.5194/isprs-archives-l-4-w2-2026-1.summary: With the increasing availability of powerful computational resources and artificial intelligence (AI), a data-driven approach has been gaining attention in atmospheric science, particularly in downscaling/emulating research. For example, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are used to emulate fine-resolution climate data fields by physics-based models. Although CNN-based downscaling has shown good performance for air temperature across various climate scales, studies at the urban scale remain limited due to the scarcity of long-term high-resolution climate data that can represent local urban effects. This study explores whether CNNs can accurately downscale/emulate urban-scale temperature distributions, with a focus on the urban heat island (UHI), using 250 m resolution Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) simulation data over Sofia, Bulgaria, as training data. Input features, including air temperature, wind components, surface solar radiation, and elevation, are used, and their impacts on targeted 250 m resolution air temperature are evaluated. The results show that, while the CNN-based approach shows promise in generating urban-scale temperature distributions, the selection/combination of input features influences downscaling performance. Warm bias exceeding +2.00 °C was almost eliminated by including all input features. The downscaled result emulated the broad spatial pattern. However, detailed spatial and temporal variability, such as UHI, was still not captured. These findings revealed that the input feature selection can influence CNN-based temperature downscaling, providing useful insight into future regional-to-microscale downscaling toward urban digital twins (UDTs).

doi:10.3390/rs18213665.title: A Comparative Study of Deep Learning Architectures for Multi-Source Precipitation Data Fusion Towards Daily Precipitation Estimation in the Yellow River Basin, China
doi:10.3390/rs18213665.summary: Accurate precipitation estimation is crucial for water management and flood reconstructions, yet remains challenging due to sparse ground observations and systematic satellite biases. Despite the rise of deep learning in multi-source fusion, controlled comparisons under a unified framework remain scarce, and the roles of window size and precipitation product combinations remain underexplored. This study evaluated five deep learning architectures, namely 1D CNN, 2D CNN, 1D–2D CNN, 3D CNN, and Transformer, for fusing three precipitation products (IMERG, MSWEP, and ERA5-Land) to estimate station-scale daily precipitation in the Yellow River Basin, China. Results showed that deep learning models consistently outperformed individual products, weighting methods, and machine learning methods, with Transformer achieving the best overall performance, followed by 3D CNN; MSWEP led the standalone products. Spatial improvements were more pronounced in densely gauged areas, but Transformer also performed well in the sparse western regions. All products and fusion models tended to overestimate no-rain and light-rain events and underestimate moderate-to-heavy, and extreme events, with Transformer yielding the largest reductions in conditional RMSE and BIAS for heavy and extreme events. Enlarging the spatial or temporal window individually improved performance, and combining both worked even better. Ablation experiments revealed that IMERG contributed little unique information, whereas incorporating more products generally improved Transformer performance. Overall, Transformer demonstrated superior performance in fusing precipitation products and enhancing estimation accuracy.

doi:10.1029/2025wr042530.title: In the Age of AI—Are National Models and Data Sets Still Important for Stream Flow Prediction?
doi:10.1029/2025wr042530.summary: Accurate streamflow prediction is critical for effective water resource management, and recent advances in deep learning and multi‐basin data sets have significantly improved model skill. Global deep‐learning models, trained on thousands of catchments have demonstrated strong generalization across diverse climates and continents. However, these models rely solely on globally available meteorological inputs, potentially overlooking the value of nationally developed data sets with enhanced regional accuracy. In this study, we assess the benefit of using Canada's high‐resolution national reanalysis data set (CaSR) in long short‐term memory (LSTM) models for streamflow prediction. We compare model performance using different meteorological forcings, global (ERA5‐Land), continental (Daymet), national (CaSR), and a combined “Complete” model, across over 1,000 Canadian stream gauges. Model performance is evaluated using the Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), Kling‐Gupta Efficiency (KGE) and related metrics. We also benchmark our best‐performing model against Google's global LSTM streamflow model at 412 Canadian gauges. Results show that national‐scale deep‐learning models using CaSR outperforms deep‐learning models using only global or continental inputs. The Complete model achieved the highest performance, with a median KGE 0.886−exceeding the 0.839 achieved by Google's global model within Canada. These findings suggest that nationally trained models using a wide array of inputs, including national meteorological data sets, can outperform state‐of‐the‐art global deep‐learning models that do not use such data when applied within their region of origin. For countries with dense observational networks and distinct hydrological regimes, investing in national data sets and models can enhance deep‐learning model prediction accuracy, leading to improved resilience to climate extremes and local water management decisions.

doi:10.1088/2515-7620/aeba46.title: Centenary evolution of rainfall datasets: a comprehensive review of gauge, radar satellite, and physics-guided machine learning-based products
doi:10.1088/2515-7620/aeba46.summary: Accurate precipitation data are crucial for understanding hydroclimatic processes to support water resource management and disaster risk reduction. This study presents a systematic review of rainfall datasets from the early 20th century to the present, emphasizing the roles of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in precipitation estimation. Unlike prior reviews that primarily catalog global precipitation datasets or examine individual ML applications, this synthesis jointly traces observing-system evolution and evaluates when ML adds demonstrable value relative to named conventional baselines. The evolution of datasets is categorized into four overlapping phases: (i) gauge-based observations, (ii) ground-based weather radar quantitative precipitation estimation (iii) satellite-era products, and (iv) modern multi-source and AI-enhanced datasets. Early gauge-based datasets, provide long-term climate records vital for historical analysis, though they are limited by sparse spatial coverage and interpolation uncertainties. Ground-based radar networks added repeated kilometer-scale mapping of storm structure, although reflectivity-to-rainfall conversion and gauge adjustment introduce their own errors. The satellite era, marked by missions such as Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission and global precipitation measurement, has significantly improved precipitation monitoring by providing near-global coverage with higher spatial and temporal resolution. However, these datasets still face challenges related to systematic biases and the representation of extreme events and complex terrains. Recent advancements highlight the important but conditional role of AI/ML techniques, including neural networks, convolutional architectures, and ensemble learning methods. Within specific study domains and validation designs, these approaches have improved precipitation estimation through applications such as satellite retrieval, bias correction, gap filling, downscaling, and multi-source data fusion. This study comparisons shows meaningful but non-universal gains: GPROF-NN reduced global precipitation measurements microwave imager retrieval mean absolute error from 0.079 to 0.043 mm h−1; a cloud-informed correction reduced IMERG early RMSE by 53%–66% in two Chinese basins and a two-step fusion framework improved modified KGE by 15%–85% across six source products. These values cannot be pooled as a formal meta-analysis because the studies use different references, climates, periods, and validation designs. The evidence does not establish universal transfer or consistent improvement in extreme-event representation; priorities are cross-region and forward-in-time validation, calibrated uncertainty quantification, and robustness under non-stationary climate conditions.

arxiv:2611.21146.title: Model-based neural network for global floodplains analysis
arxiv:2611.21146.summary: We address the super-resolution of multispectral remote sensing imagery for long-term floodplain monitoring, enhancing Landsat acquisitions towards Sentinel-2 resolution. Exploiting the period during which both missions observed the same areas, we build DLhasa-L2S , to our knowledge the first paired dataset dedicated to multispectral super-resolution for river analysis. It covers the Lhasa River (Tibet), whose strong anthropogenic changes and diverse hydromorphological profiles make it an ideal study area. We developed two model-based neural networks: a forward-backward (FB) plug-and-play scheme and an unfolded FB scheme. We compared them against learned neural networks baselines (SwinIR, RDN) on synthetic data, on real scenes, and through a statistical test over the whole real paired Landsat-Sentinel dataset. The unfolded network achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM on the real RGB components with fast inference, offering the best trade-off between accuracy and computational cost. For NDWI-based water segmentation, its performance shows no statistically significant difference from that of the best methods.

doi:10.3390/geomatics6050115.title: A Hybrid ConvNeXt, Dual-Transformer, and U-Net Architecture for Direct Satellite-Based Precipitation Estimation from MSG/SEVIRI
doi:10.3390/geomatics6050115.summary: Accurate quantification of precipitation is critical for anticipating extreme cli mate events such as droughts and flash floods, yet ground rain gauges and weather radars in Northern Algeria suffer from limited spatial coverage and high maintenance costs. Satellite remote sensing via Meteosat Second Generation (MSG/SEVIRI) multispectral imagery offers optimal spatio-temporal coverage, but converting indirect cloud-top properties into direct rainfall rates remains challenging. To overcome the limitations of standard machine learning and conventional convolutional neural networks in modeling long-range atmospheric dependencies, this study proposes a novel end-to-end hybrid deep learning architecture, combining ConvNeXt, Dual-Transformer, and U-Net models, for direct pixel-wise precipitation regression without intermediate classification. The model leverages a ConvNeXt backbone with large-kernel depthwise convolutions for local spatial feature extraction, a Dual-Transformer module utilizing parallel spatial and spectral attention to capture non-local cloud structures, and a U-Net decoder with multi-scale skip connections for high-resolution rainfall reconstruction. Trained and validated against reference target fields constructed from weather radar and rain gauge fusion covering 2006–2012, the proposed ConvNeXt + Dual-Transformer + U-Net framework demonstrates superior performance over traditional machine learning baselines (RF, MLP, SVM) and standard CNN architectures (U-Net, ConvNeXt + U-Net). The model effectively reduces heteroscedastic error dispersion, achieving Pearson correlation coefficients (R) of 0.78 for instantaneous estimates, 0.84 for 3 h accumulations, 0.89 for daily totals, and 0.96 at the weekly scale, alongside lower root mean square errors (RMSE = 12.4 mm/day) and a minimal bias (0.1 mm/week). These results confirm that integrating global attention mechanisms with convolutional backbones enhances the modeling of complex convective rainfall, providing a robust operational tool for continuous satellite-based precipitation retrieval over Northern Algeria.

doi:10.1088/2515-7620/aeb47d.title: An optimized hybrid deep learning framework for short-range rainfall forecasting in Mumbai’s monsoon regime
doi:10.1088/2515-7620/aeb47d.summary: Short-range rainfall forecasting in tropical coastal megacities is a formidable challenge owing to the nonlinear dynamics, strong seasonality, and pronounced interannual variability that characterize monsoon precipitation regimes. This study develops and evaluates deep learning frameworks for multi-lead-time (D + 1 to D + 4) daily rainfall forecasting over Mumbai (72.88° E, 19.07° N), India, a densely populated coastal metropolis where accurate precipitation prediction is directly consequential for flood early warning. Six forecasting systems namely Random Forest, XGBoost, a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN), a Transformer, and two metaheuristically tuned variants of a novel Conv1D–CBAM–BiLSTM–attention Enhanced Hybrid architecture (genetic algorithms (GA)-Hybrid and PSO-Enhanced) are benchmarked against persistence and climatology references. The PSO-Enhanced ensemble is the strongest system at every lead, attaining R2 = 0.636 (RMSE = 8.97 mm d−1) at D + 1 and 0.454, 0.373 and 0.399 at D + 2D + 4, ahead of the GA-Hybrid (0.626, 0.428, 0.352, 0.385), the strongest gradient-boosting benchmark XGBoost (R2 ⩽ 0.561), persistence (R2 = 0.572 at D + 1, declining to 0.049 by D + 4), and climatology (R2 = 0.327, lead-independent). Recurrent-memory architectures outperform the memoryless CNN and Transformer at every lead, indicating that sequential dependence, rather than attention alone, carries most of the exploitable predictive signal. For detection of rainfall exceeding the 95th percentile, the two optimized hybrids achieve the highest critical success index at every lead (up to 0.403 at D + 1), considerably exceeding persistence, whose detection skill collapses beyond D + 2. SHAP attribution shows that D + 1 skill rests chiefly on rainfall persistence and 850–500 hPa moisture, whose combined importance nearly halves by D + 2. Benchmarked against GraphCast and NOAA GFS for June–September 2019, the PSO-Enhanced framework trails the global systems at short lead but attains higher correlation with observations by D + 4 (r = 0.61 versus 0.32 and 0.25, respectively), indicating a comparative advantage of the localized, predictor-rich statistical approach at longer point-forecast horizons.
