doi:10.1007/s44288-026-00775-0.title: An observational perspective on extreme precipitation indices over the mountainous regions of Northwest Himalaya
doi:10.1007/s44288-026-00775-0.summary: The Northwest Himalaya region is highly susceptible to extreme rainfall events due to its steep topography and complex climatic variability, which can trigger significant hydro-meteorological hazards, including heavy snowfall, hailstorms, floods, and droughts. The erratic precipitation patterns, both in the short and long term, exacerbate these hazards. Furthermore, climate change is amplifying the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, thereby increasing the vulnerability of the region and posing substantial challenges for infrastructure resilience, agricultural sustainability, and effective disaster management. This study utilizes the High Asia Refined Analysis version 2 dataset (HARv2), a high-resolution (10 km) WRF model output, spanning 1981–2020, to analyze precipitation trends across three sub-regions — Jammu & Kashmir (JK), Himachal Pradesh (HP), and Uttarakhand (UK) — validated against IMD and IMDAA datasets. All extreme precipitation indices as defined by the Expert Team on Climate Change Detection and Indices (ETCCDI) have been used for the study. ERA5 and HARv2 derived VIMT analysis is done for large-scale moisture influx understanding, and the role of ENSO in driving moisture transport is examined. JK exhibits the most pronounced drying signal, with statistically significant declines across multiple precipitation indices, while increasing CDD over both JK and HP indicates growing drought risk. UK shows no significant trends, reflecting the dominant role of orographic processes in its precipitation regime. A distinct spatial gradient in precipitation-generating mechanisms is identified — from synoptic-dynamic control over JK to orographic dominance over UK, with HP representing a transitional regime. With multiple diagnostic variables evaluated, it is concluded that moisture alone does not explain precipitation extremes in the NWH, and that orographic uplift and synoptic-scale disturbances are equally important drivers. The findings highlight the need for targeted climate change mitigation strategies and region-specific resource allocation to protect the vulnerable Himalayan region.

doi:10.3390/rs18203593.title: Spatial Super-Resolution of Satellite-Derived SST Data via Generative Adversarial Networks in the Mediterranean Sea
doi:10.3390/rs18203593.summary: In this work, we compare deep convolutional and generative models to improve the reconstruction of sea surface temperature (SST) gradients and effective resolution from cloud-contaminated satellite infrared data. Standard gap-filling techniques produce spatially complete datasets, but they inherently smooth out fine-scale features and gradients that may be critical for a better understanding of the ocean dynamics. Here, we investigate how the use of deep learning models as Autoencoders (AEs) and generative models as Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (C-GANs) differently contribute to recovering the small-scale structures lost during interpolation. Our supervised, observation-based training relies on satellite-derived SST data from the Mediterranean Sea, with a focus on learning the statistical relationship between high-resolution fields and their low-resolution counterparts. We apply a tiling and merging strategy to deal with limited observational coverage and to ensure spatial continuity. Quantitative validation based on mean squared error metrics, spectral analysis, and gradient statistics shows that the AE reduces the reconstruction error, but it fails to recover high-frequency variability. In contrast, the C-GAN effectively restores the statistical properties of the true SST field at the cost of increasing the pointwise discrepancy with the ground truth observations. Our results highlight the potential of deep models to enhance the physical and statistical realism of gap-filled satellite data in oceanographic applications.

doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0343910.title: Summer seasonal precipitation prediction in the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River using neural network approaches
doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0343910.summary: Accurate prediction of summer precipitation is essential for agricultural planning and flood prevention. However, precipitation is strongly nonlinear. In the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River (MLYR), many interacting factors and large interannual variability make conventional forecasting methods unreliable. This study proposes neural network approaches to address this challenge. We select independent predictors from 130 circulation indices of the National Climate Center (NCC) and from the ERA5 monthly dataset, including sea surface temperature (SST), 500 hPa geopotential height, and land surface variables. Predictors are chosen through correlation, partial correlation, and autocorrelation analyses. They are then processed with detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA), standardization, and normalization. Four models are trained: a back propagation (BP) network, a gated recurrent unit (GRU) network, a coupled BP-GRU network, and a particle swarm optimization (PSO)-optimized coupled BP-GRU network. A strict chronological split is used (training: 1980–2000; validation: 2001–2010; testing: 2011–2024). Results are reported as the mean ± standard deviation over ten independent runs. The PSO-optimized coupled network performs best (test MSE = 0.0177 ± 0.0106; spatial correlation r = 0.44). It outperforms the standalone GRU (MSE = 0.0207 ± 0.0003), the coupled BP-GRU (MSE = 0.0357 ± 0.0175), and the standalone BP model (MSE = 0.0447 ± 0.0212). It is also the only network to beat the climatological baseline (MSE = 0.0181). The GRU is the most stable across runs but reproduces spatial patterns poorly. Overall, combining recurrent architectures with physical predictors through evolutionary optimization improves seasonal prediction. However, all models show limited skill (R2 near zero), reflecting the difficulty of this task. The approach offers a reference for flood-season forecasting in the MLYR, with potential use in agriculture and flood prevention.

doi:10.1109/jstars.2026.3746867.title: A Progressive Downscaling Framework With Hybrid Attention Mechanisms for High-Resolution Soil Moisture Estimation
doi:10.1109/jstars.2026.3746867.summary: Soil moisture is a critical variable regulating terrestrial water and energy exchange, with broad applications in drought monitoring, water resources management, and climate change research. However, passive microwave soil moisture products are often constrained by coarse spatial resolution, limiting their utility for regional- and local-scale applications. To address this challenge, we propose a progressive downscaling framework with hybrid attention mechanisms (PDHAM) to generate high-resolution soil moisture estimates. The framework progressively downscales soil moisture through two cascaded stages, first from 0.36° to 0.06° and then from 0.06° to 0.01°, thereby improving downscaling robustness. Each stage incorporates a hybrid attention module to enhance the extraction of spatial details. The effectiveness of PDHAM was evaluated using in situ observations across mainland China. PDHAM consistently outperformed a backpropagation neural network, a deep belief network, and a residual dense network, achieving an average correlation coefficient of 0.72 and an unbiased root-mean-square error of 0.061 m3/m3. Moreover, the downscaled results compared favorably with two existing high-resolution soil moisture datasets. These findings demonstrate the strong potential of PDHAM to improve fine-scale soil moisture monitoring and support hydrological, agricultural, and climatological applications.

doi:10.1029/2026jh001372.title: A Super‐Resolution Model for Enhancing the Intensity and Structure of Tropical Cyclone Predictions
doi:10.1029/2026jh001372.summary: Accurate predictions of intensity and structure of tropical cyclones (TCs) are crucial for disaster warning, prevention and mitigation. Traditional dynamical models with coarse horizontal resolutions suffer from systematic underprediction of TC intensity, whereas those with fine horizontal resolutions require intensive computations. Deep learning (DL)‐based models are computationally efficient yet substantially underpredict the TC intensity. To enhance the prediction of DL‐based weather models for TC intensities and structures, a hybrid framework (HybSR‐TC) is proposed here. By integrating a Swin Transformer backbone with multi‐variable processing and meta‐upsampling techniques, HybSR‐TC is trained based on low‐resolution (0.25°) forecasts of Pangu‐Weather and high‐resolution (2 km) weather research and forecasting forecasts with accurate TC tracks and well simulated intensities and structures. For TC predictions, HybSR‐TC maps the 6‐hr Pangu‐Weather forecasts of surface pressure and wind fields at 0.25° resolution to 2‐km resolution fields without the requirement for massive computational costs. HybSR‐TC can better capture the rapid intensification and temporal evolution of TCs than Pangu‐Weather and bilinear interpolation. HybSR‐TC produces significantly smaller errors of TC intensity and structure than Pangu‐Weather and bilinear interpolation, until approximately 10‐day lead times. Thus, the ability of HybSR‐TC to enhance the forecasts of TC intensity and structure based on the low‐resolution forecasts from AI models has been demonstrated.

doi:10.1109/lgrs.2026.3735399.title: OSISAF-to-MASAM2: Deep Learning for Sea Ice Concentration Super-Resolution Product
doi:10.1109/lgrs.2026.3735399.summary: This letter presents a deep learning approach for Arctic sea ice concentration (SIC) downscaling based on multisensor fusion applied during the model training stage. While conventional downscaling methods primarily enhance spatial resolution, the proposed approach also improves physical consistency by fusing the widely used Ocean and Sea Ice Satellite Application Facility (OSISAF) SIC dataset with the high-resolution multisensor-corrected MASAM2 product. This synthesis not only increases spatial resolution from 25 to 4 km, but also yields more realistic ice patterns, as validated by a high structural similarity metric and a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.02. A comparison of U-Net-based and attention U-Net architectures with classical interpolation methods, a conditional diffusion baseline, and a manual hybrid approach demonstrates the advantages of the proposed solution. The projection change between the two products is embedded in the network as a fixed resampling layer, removing the external remapping stage from the pipeline. The presented model has strong potential to improve sea ice forecasting quality and generate high-resolution historical datasets. Code and weights are provided on https://github.com/ITMO-NSS-team/GRSL_masam2_downscaling

doi:10.1029/2026jh001400.title: HiResCastNet: A 3D Deep Learning Model for Probabilistic Regional High‐Resolution Subseasonal Forecasting Through Downscaling
doi:10.1029/2026jh001400.summary: High‐resolution subseasonal forecasts, spanning two to 6 weeks, play a vital role in bridging the gap between short‐range forecasts and seasonal predictions. They provide crucial information for decision‐making in disaster and hazard preparedness, early warning systems, water resource management, and renewable energy. However, generating subseasonal forecasts at high spatial and temporal resolutions remains a significant challenge. Global subseasonal forecasting systems such as European Center for Medium‐Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) typically provide outputs at a coarse spatial resolution of about 31 km and a temporal resolution of 12 hr, which limits their usefulness for regional‐scale planning and impact assessments. Our three‐dimensional (3D) high‐resolution regional subseasonal forecasts are generated by dynamically downscaling the ECMWF subseasonal forecasts using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model, producing outputs at a spatial resolution of 4 km and a temporal resolution of 3 hr. Yet, the dynamical downscaling model is computationally very demanding, especially when using multiple ensemble members. To address this limitation, we introduce HiResCastNet, a data‐driven, probabilistic downscaling framework combining Swin‐transformer and a diffusion model, which serves as an efficient surrogate for the traditional downscaling system. HiResCastNet takes spatio‐temporal coarse resolution forecasts from ECMWF subseasonal system as inputs, and generates 3D high‐resolution forecasts at 4 km spatial resolution and 3‐hourly intervals. Our results suggest that HiResCastNet significantly reduces computational cost while maintaining strong agreement with WRF physical model. It reproduces the dynamical behavior across variables such as wind and temperature and handles the downscaling of multiple ensemble members efficiently, which highlights its potential for operational use.

doi:10.1029/2026jh001290.title: High‐Resolution Downscaling of a Lightweight Climate Emulator Using Diffusion‐Based Super‐Resolution
doi:10.1029/2026jh001290.summary: High‐resolution climate fields are essential for the assessment of their regional and local effects. Current global climate models, along with being computationally expensive, are often too coarse for applications that depend on local extremes and orographic gradients. Machine learning offers a computationally efficient route for both climate emulation and super‐resolution from coarse simulations to finer spatial scales. Therefore, we develop a data‐driven downscaling framework for the Lightweight Uncoupled ClImate Emulator (LUCIE), a lightweight Spherical Fourier Neural Operator climate emulator introduced by Guan et al. (2025, https://doi.org/10.1029/2025ms005152 ). We compare deterministic super‐resolution baselines, including a U‐Net and Spherical Fourier Neural Operator (SFNO), with two probabilistic diffusion formulations: a conditional Elucidated Diffusion Model and a diffusion‐posterior‐sampling approach. The models are trained on 6‐hourly ERA5 reanalysis fields from 2000 to 2009 and evaluated on out‐of‐sample LUCIE predictions from 2010 to 2018, downscaling coarse emulator states to km resolution. Performance is assessed against ERA5 using latitude‐weighted root mean square error (RMSE), power spectra, probability density functions, and the leading Empirical Orthogonal Function of zonal wind. These diagnostics test whether deterministic and probabilistic super‐resolution models can recover fine‐scale climatological statistics, high‐wavenumber variability, and dominant modes with an imperfect coarse emulator. Our results characterize the strengths and limitations of emulator‐driven super‐resolution, including its ability to reproduce ERA5‐like fine‐scale statistics while preserving explicit coarse‐scale consistency with LUCIE.

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-80185-x.title: Trade-offs in deep learning approaches for precipitation downscaling across weather regimes
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-80185-x.summary: Accurate high-resolution precipitation information is critical for assessing hydrological extremes and climate change impacts in complex topographic regions. While machine learning-based downscaling provides a computationally efficient alternative to dynamical models, its performance can depend on regional climate characteristics and terrain complexity. In this study, we systematically benchmarked representative deep learning approaches for daily statistical downscaling over Japan, including quantile-based and stochastic CNN formulations, two- (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) U-Net variants, and a diffusion-based generative model, alongside conventional baselines. Model performance was evaluated using comprehensive statistical and spatial metrics under both climatological and typhoon-affected conditions, enabling us to assess model robustness under extreme precipitation regimes. We further developed a proof-of-concept forecasting configuration for 3D U-Net prediction of next-day precipitation from short predictor sequences, together with an extreme super-resolution experiment to assess scalability to very high target resolutions. The results revealed clear trade-offs: quantile mapping best reproduced distributional properties, deterministic CNNs performed particularly well for standard deterministic metrics, the stochastic CNN achieved the highest average neighborhood-scale skill, and the diffusion model best reproduced the spatial power spectrum, while U-Nets tended to smooth small scales. Nevertheless, the asymmetric-loss U-Net provided the most robust performance during typhoon conditions. These findings provide practical guidance for model selection in complex climatic regions and illustrate how inductive biases interact with regional climate dynamics.

doi:10.1029/2026ea005059.title: Zero‐Shot Transferability of Deep Learning Models for Precipitation Super‐Resolution Across Diverse Climate Regimes
doi:10.1029/2026ea005059.summary: High‐resolution precipitation fields are essential for characterizing climate extremes, assessing sectoral impacts, and improving early warning systems. However, the resolution of global Earth system models (ESMs) and numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems remains limited by computational constraints. This study assesses the zero‐shot transferability of deep learning (DL)‐based super‐resolution (SR) models for precipitation across diverse geographic domains, data sources, and temporal scales. A suite of DL‐based SR architectures, ranging from convolutional baselines to spatial‐attention‐based generative models, is trained on a limited regional observational record of satellite‐derived precipitation from three monsoon‐dominated regions of the Indian subcontinent during 2001–2014. DL model generalization is assessed through out‐of‐sample transfer across climatically diverse domains using observations (2015–2023), NWP forecasts (2018–2023), and a 150‐year ESM simulation spanning 1950–2100, all without retraining or fine‐tuning. Across tropical, subtropical, and mid‐latitude climate regimes, the models show strong zero‐shot transferability, achieving Kling‐Gupta efficiency (KGE) scores approximately 0.85 or higher. Skill gains are evident in fine‐scale spatial variability and extreme precipitation statistics that are poorly represented in the coarse‐resolution inputs. Cross‐source application to weather forecasts and long‐term climate simulations further demonstrates the applicability of SR models across differing forcing data and evolving climate conditions. While differences among architectures are generally modest, spatial attention‐based models show enhanced performance in spatial fidelity and extreme‐event detection. This framework does not explicitly represent the physical processes governing precipitation formation or enforce physical constraints; within these limitations, its performance under our validation strategy indicates robustness and utility as an efficient post‐processing tool for weather and climate models.

doi:10.5194/gmd-19-9235-2026.title: China regional 3 km downscaling based on residual Corrective Diffusion model
doi:10.5194/gmd-19-9235-2026.summary: A fundamental challenge in numerical weather prediction is efficiently producing high-resolution forecasts. A widely adopted solution is to downscale coarser global model outputs. This study focuses on statistical downscaling, which uses historical data to learn mappings between low- and high-resolution meteorological fields. Deep learning has become a key tool for this, enabling powerful super-resolution models like diffusion models and Generative Adversarial Networks for downscaling applications. Herein, we leverage CorrDiff, a diffusion-based downscaling framework, with three key enhancements relative to its original implementation. First, the study domain is expanded to nearly 40 times the spatial extent of the original version. Second, the scope of target downscaling variables is extended beyond surface variables to incorporate upper-air variables across six pressure levels. Third, a global residual connection is integrated to further boost prediction accuracy. To produce 3 km resolution forecasts for the China region, the trained CorrDiff model is applied to 25 km global grid forecasts derived from two sources: a conventional global numerical weather prediction model and a deep learning-based weather model developed using Spherical Fourier Neural Operators. The China Meteorological Administration Mesoscale Model (CMA-MESO) is selected as the baseline for comparative evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that the downscaled forecasts generated by our framework outperform the direct forecasts of CMA-MESO for almost all target variables, as quantified by the Mean Absolute Error metric. Specifically, forecasts of radar composite reflectivity reveal that CorrDiff, as a generative model, is capable of capturing fine-grained meteorological details, yielding more physically realistic predictions than deterministic regression-based downscaling models.

arxiv:2609.39833.title: RainAtlas: A Multi-Continental Dataset for Precipitation Downscaling
arxiv:2609.39833.summary: Extreme rainfall events are increasing in intensity and frequency as climate change accelerates. While kilometer-scale precipitation forecasts are critical for supporting local decision-making, the limited availability of high-resolution precipitation observations hinders their accuracy, especially in under-resourced regions. Machine learning models are widely used to downscale precipitation data to km-scale, but their application to unseen geographies presents challenges. First, processing raw high-resolution precipitation datasets across regions requires significant engineering and domain expertise. Second, generalization across regions remains difficult. To help overcome these barriers, we release RainAtlas, a large-scale, ML-ready and multi-continental dataset for precipitation downscaling. Covering three continents, RainAtlas harmonizes heterogeneous hourly km-scale observations to a common 2-km grid. Each regional partition contains around 210,000 aligned low- and high-resolution precipitation pairs, respectively from ERA5 reanalysis and direct observations. We benchmark state-of-the-art ML-based downscaling models across RainAtlas using a wide range of metrics. Our evaluation reveals substantial variance in out-of-domain generalization depending on the training regions. This underscores the need for cross-regional, multi-source km-scale evaluation, establishing RainAtlas as a well-positioned benchmark for precipitation downscaling research.

doi:10.1117/12.3131069.title: A physics-informed neural network for downscaling ERA5 reanalysis sea surface temperature to kilometre-scale resolution
doi:10.1117/12.3131069.summary: Sea surface temperature (SST) from ERA5 reanalysis (0.25° × 0.25°) is too coarse to resolve fronts and mesoscale eddies in coastal waters. Here we construct a physics-informed neural network (PINN) that embeds the ocean advection–diffusion equation as a training constraint. The network takes spatiotemporal coordinates as input, uses coarse ERA5 SST as supervised labels, and outputs physically consistent high-resolution SST. Applied to daily ERA5 data over the Yellow Sea for 2021, the model downscales SST from 0.25° to 5 km resolution. Applied to daily ERA5 data over the Yellow Sea for 2021, the model downscales SST from 0.25° to 5 km resolution with a root-mean-square error of 0.94 °C and R2 of 0.92. This model outperforms traditional methods such as bilinear interpolation. It also preserves thermodynamically consistent fine-scale structures at temperature fronts and water-mass boundaries. This framework offers a physically credible route for generating high-resolution coastal reanalysis datasets and is extensible to other ocean variables.

arxiv:2610.03757.title: Generalizable Neural Downscaling of Earth System Model Wind Fields via Continuous Dynamics Modeling
arxiv:2610.03757.summary: Accurate high-resolution wind field simulations are critical for resolving fine-scale atmospheric dynamics, yet the simulation of wind fields in Earth System Models (ESMs) remains limited by coarse spatial resolution and systematic biases. To address this, data-driven down scaling techniques have been widely used to enhance coarse-resolution ESM outputs. However, existing methods are typically tied to fixed discretizations, limiting generalization across models with different native resolutions. Here we formulate global near-surface wind downscaling as an operator-learning problem on continuous atmospheric state fields and develop a downscaling neural operator that maps coarse-scale fields to fine-scale counterparts across heterogeneous discretizations. The operator learning-based neural downscaling framework outperforms dominant baselines, recovers fine-scale physical structures, and generalizes to previously unseen ESMs and future climate scenarios without retraining, while preserving long-term wind projection trends. These findings establish a generalizable paradigm for high-resolution climate downscaling across diverse simulation outputs and future scenarios.

doi:10.3390/cli14110233.title: AI-Based Super-Resolution Approaches to Reconstruct Temperature Fields of Climatic Data Using Deep Neural Networks
doi:10.3390/cli14110233.summary: High-fidelity climate analysis is heavily constrained both by the computational costs of high-resolution dynamical simulations and by the general scarcity of fine-scale observational data for model evaluation. To address these limitations, in this work we propose a deep learning framework for spatial climate downscaling using an AI-based super-resolution (SR) approach. We develop Deep Neural Network architectures designed to upscale 2 m surface temperature fields, bridging the gap between gridded global reanalysis data at lower scale (1.0°) and higher scale (0.25°). We developed three DNN models, specifically ResNet, RNN, and ConvRNN, trained and validated on ECMWF ERA5 data from the early years of the current millennium (i.e., 01/01,01/04,01/07,01/10 of 2001,2003,2005 at 00:00) and evaluated over various periods, including 1992, a historical period influenced by the 1991 Mount Pinatubo eruption (a large volcanic eruption which is known to have had impacts on the climate due to the massive stratospheric injections of sulfur dioxide). The framework is tested also on the Berkeley Earth global observational dataset and on outputs from a MPI-ESM1-2-LR historical global climate simulation and compared with traditional interpolation methods, to verify the models generalization capability. The models reached high levels of accuracy, with errors lower than 0.5 K and a similarity index higher than 0.97, successfully capturing the spatio-temporal dynamics of temperature fields. Overall, the novelty of this work is in three main aspects: the implementation of DNN capable to capture the spatio-temporal dynamics and not only the static frame-by-frame processes, the combination of conventional pixel-based error metrics with morphological validation frameworks based on isoline pattern and gradient orientation comparison, and the introduction of optimized training strategies (i.e., early stopping), to improve learning mechanisms and balance computational costs.

arxiv:2607.17037.title: Apeliotes: A Diffusion-Based Modeling Framework for km-scale Multi-Level Atmospheric Fields
arxiv:2607.17037.summary: High-resolution atmospheric data are required to resolve mesoscale and localized meteorological structures, however, such datasets remain limited in many regions of the world. Existing high-resolution weather products are typically produced through dynamical downscaling, which is computationally expensive and difficult to scale across locations, variables, and forecast scenarios. These limitations motivate machine-learning-based downscaling systems that can generate multiple weather variables stochastically while producing new high-resolution fields directly. In this paper we present Apeliotes, a framework for high-resolution weather forecasting. Built on the global re-analysis atmospheric data, a pre-trained global weather foundation model, and a regionally trained generative diffusion model, Apeliotes not only provides accurate kilometer-scale weather variables, but also multi-level atmospheric fields which are not directly available in the existing global atmospheric data. Our comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that Apeliotes achieves highly competitive performance. The model predicts vertical wind profile with less than 3% error between truth and predicted fields, achieving correlations of 0.91 for 10-m wind speed and 0.99 for 2-m temperature, with NRMSE values of 0.42 and 0.17, respectively.

doi:10.5194/essd-18-7593-2026.title: High-resolution global groundwater storage anomalies: a 1 km downscaled dataset
doi:10.5194/essd-18-7593-2026.summary: Groundwater depletion poses a challenge to water security, but the coarse spatial resolution of Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) observations limits the characterization of groundwater variability at regional and local scales. Here, we present a 1 km monthly global groundwater storage anomaly (GWSA) dataset covering April 2002–December 2020. The dataset was generated using Singular Spectrum Analysis (SSA) for temporal gap filling, 19 high-resolution hydroclimatic and geophysical predictors, and aquifer-stratified machine-learning downscaling. Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and deep neural networks (DNN) were evaluated as candidate models, and XGBoost was selected for dataset production based on internal, cross-scale, and in-situ evaluations. When aggregated to the original GRACE scale, the 1 km product agreed closely with the original GWSA ( R 2 = 0.972, RMSE = 2.10 cm). Independent evaluation used a global archive of 152 069 groundwater-monitoring wells and a 1° spatial-block calibration–validation design. Effective specific yield ( S yeff ) was estimated from calibration blocks and transferred to held-out blocks before comparison at a common 0.25° grid. For XGBoost, the held-out evaluation yielded R 2 = 0.538, RMSE = 0.378 cm yr −1 , and Bias = 0.106 cm yr −1 . The association between modeled and observation-derived trends remained similar under ± 30 % perturbations in S yeff , although amplitude-related metrics were more sensitive to the conversion coefficient. Standardized time-series comparisons and monthly evaluations of representative aquifers showed better agreement for long-term variability than for seasonal variability. Comparisons with published regional estimates showed close agreement in the North China Plain, weaker depletion magnitudes in northwestern India and California, and a trend-sign mismatch in the High Plains Aquifer during 2003–2013. Experiments using CSR, JPL, H08, and WaterGAP also showed that reconstruction performance and predictor importance depend on the target product. The dataset provides kilometre-scale estimates of groundwater-storage variability under the large-scale GRACE constraint. Local interpretation of the reconstructed spatial patterns requires additional groundwater-level, abstraction, and hydrogeological observations. The 1 km monthly global GWSA dataset is openly available from the National Cryosphere Desert Data Center at https://doi.org/10.12072/ncdc.hydrology.db7323.2026 (Fan et al., 2026).

doi:10.1007/s12665-026-13186-8.title: Enhancing GRACE-derived terrestrial water storage estimates through bias-corrected downscaling using machine learning and artificial bee colony optimization
doi:10.1007/s12665-026-13186-8.summary: Accurate monitoring of spatiotemporal variations of Terrestrial Water Storage (TWS) is essential for sustainable water resources management in arid and semi-arid regions. The Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) and GRACE-Follow On (GRACE-FO) satellite missions serve as valuable tools for estimating changes in TWS; however, their coarse spatial resolution poses challenges for applications at local and regional scales. In this study, downscaling of the GRACE data for the Yazd province, Iran, was conducted using three Machine Learning (ML) models, including Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and two Deep Neural Networks, i.e., DNN1 and DNN2, while the latter has more hidden layers than the former. To enhance accuracy and reduce the systematic bias in the model outputs, the Artificial Bee Colony (ABC) metaheuristic algorithm and a hybrid version combining ABC and Quantile Mapping were employed as the bias correction framework. The input data for the models were derived from high-resolution datasets, including CHIRPS for precipitation and TerraClimate for climatic variables listed in Table 1. The performance evaluation of the models, based on statistical indices, indicated that the XGBoost model achieved the highest accuracy in reproducing TWS anomalies (R2 = 0.829) and the lowest error among the ML models. The implementation of the ABC algorithm resulted in a 12.45% reduction in root mean square errors (RMSE) and improved the consistency between model outputs and observations from piezometer wells. Temporal and spatial analyses demonstrate a continuous decline in equivalent water thickness over the past two decades, confirming a severe depletion of groundwater resources in Yazd. The findings of this study demonstrate that the integration of ML models with ABC can enhance model performance by reducing prediction errors and serve as an effective approach for generating higher-resolution GRACE-derived TWS estimates at the local scale, thereby supporting more informed water resources management decisions in arid regions. Improved downscaling of GRACE-derived using XGBoost, deep learning and multi-layer perceptron models to produce higher-resolution Terrestrial Water Storage maps in Yazd Province. Utilized high-resolution datasets, including CHIRPS and TerraClimate, as main inputs for the downscaling models. Reduced model bias and enhanced agreement with piezometer observations wells using the Artificial Bee Colony algorithm.

doi:10.1109/isctis70043.2026.11572552.title: A Convolutional Neural Network-Based Statistical Downscaling Study of ERA5 Air Temperature at the Station Scale
doi:10.1109/isctis70043.2026.11572552.summary: To evaluate the performance of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) in the station-scale application of reanalysis data, this study conducts a statistical downscaling investigation of ERA5 temperature data, using Macau as a case study. A spatiotemporally matched dataset was constructed using hourly ERA5 reanalysis data and surface observation station records from 2012 to 2022. A lightweight CNN model was developed, employing the grid fields surrounding the stations as inputs and the measured station temperatures as outputs. To investigate the influence of spatial feature extraction ranges on model performance, the downscaling effects were comparatively analyzed across four input window sizes (11 × 11, 21 × 21, 31 × 31, and 41 × 41). Simultaneously, nearest neighbor interpolation, bilinear interpolation, and cubic spline interpolation were introduced as baseline methods. Multi-dimensional evaluations were performed using Mean Squared Error (MSE), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and Correlation Coefficient (CC). The experimental results demonstrate that the CNN model effectively captures spatial correlations between grid points, with accuracy significantly surpassing that of traditional interpolation methods. Furthermore, the model performance varied with the size of the input window, confirming the critical importance of the spatial domain extent for local temperature estimation. This study indicates that the lightweight CNN provides an efficient and feasible solution for the station-scale downscaling of ERA5 data, serving as a reference for the refined application of meteorological elements in coastal regions with complex underlying surfaces.

doi:10.3390/hydrology13110307.title: Evaluating the Long-Term Robustness of Hybrid Deep Learning Models for Streamflow Projections Under Climate Change
doi:10.3390/hydrology13110307.summary: Data-driven models can help represent hydrological processes at the basin scale and predict future conditions, particularly in basins where information on physical characteristics is limited. Although these models have long been used in hydrological modeling, their reliability for long-term projections under changing climatic conditions remains insufficiently understood. This study evaluates the long-term robustness and projection consistency of data-driven algorithms under climate-change conditions using two hybrid deep learning architectures: (1) a Wavelet Transform–Deep Neural Network (WT–DNN) and (2) a Convolutional Neural Network–Long Short-Term Memory–Attention Block (CNN–LSTM–AB). It also investigates whether synthetic data augmentation using a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) during model training improves predictive performance. The study used hydrological and climatic data, including streamflow, precipitation, minimum temperature, and maximum temperature, from the Yamula Reservoir Basin, a semi-arid agricultural basin in Türkiye. The models were trained and validated for monthly streamflow using climate data from the HadGEM2–ES global circulation model for the 2000–2020 period. Long-term streamflow projections for 2021–2098 were then generated under the RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 scenarios. Model performance and robustness were assessed through sensitivity analysis, comparison of models trained with and without GAN-based data augmentation, comparison with long short-term memory (LSTM) and other recently proposed hybrid deep learning architectures, and evaluation of long-term projections against those generated by the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) under the same future climate conditions. The results showed that WT–DNN and CNN–LSTM–AB achieved higher test-period performance than the other evaluated approaches. GAN-based data augmentation further improved model performance, reducing test root mean square error (RMSE) by 34–73% and increasing Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) by up to 0.39. However, when applied to long-term climate projections, the relative performance of the models changed, and the superior performance of the proposed models during the historical period was not consistently maintained. The relationship between historical test performance and long-term agreement with SWAT also varied across performance metrics and climate scenarios, with no metric showing a significant relationship under both RCP4.5 and RCP8.5. These findings indicate that high test-period accuracy alone may not provide sufficient evidence of model robustness for long-term climate-change applications.

doi:10.1108/ijccsm-09-2025-0332.title: Unlocking wind energy potential in data-scarce regions: a deep learning framework for strategic climate action in Vietnam’s Central Highlands
doi:10.1108/ijccsm-09-2025-0332.summary: As Vietnam accelerates its transition toward a sustainable energy future under ambitious national strategies like the Power Development Plan VIII (PDP8), a critical barrier persists: the lack of high-fidelity resource maps for strategic planning. This is particularly acute in data-scarce regions with high potential, such as Vietnam’s Central Highlands. This study aims to address this strategic gap by developing and validating a robust deep learning framework to produce an enhanced and detailed high-resolution wind energy map for this region, providing a conservative proof-of-concept for regional energy planning. The framework integrates coarse-resolution daily wind speed data from an ensemble of 11 global climate models with long-term observational records (1985–2023) from a sparse network of meteorological stations. To preserve synoptic extremes critical for wind power, the downscaling was conducted at a daily temporal resolution. A suite of advanced machine learning and deep learning models were systematically trained. To address the limitations of spatial interpolation in complex terrain, the downscaled 10 m wind speeds were extrapolated to a 149 m commercial hub-height using a terrain-aware power law, integrating high-resolution surface roughness data. A technical potential map (GWh/km²/year) was then generated by combining the turbine power curve (Enercon E-101) with a GIS-based availability index (AI), factoring in constraints such as elevation, slope, land cover and urban buffers. Deep learning architectures, particularly the convolutional neural network and XGBoost, significantly outperformed traditional models, achieving R-Pearson correlation coefficients exceeding 0.85 on daily predictions. Validation against ERA5 reanalysis data demonstrated that our ML-downscaled outputs substantially reduced severe negative biases present in ERA5 over complex terrain. The framework generated one of the most detailed wind energy maps for the region, identifying specific “hotspots” capable of generating significant yields (>6.0 GWh/km²/year) while strictly masking physically constrained zones. Projections under future shared socioeconomic pathways indicate that this wind resource potential is expected to remain robust. This study could provide a powerful, replicable methodological blueprint for de-risking renewable energy investment in data-scarce regions. By embedding high-resolution spatial covariates (DEM, roughness) into the vertical extrapolation rather than relying solely on 2D interpolation, it delivers an early, scientifically rigorous tool to guide national energy policy, optimize land-use planning and accelerate the sustainable expansion of wind energy for other regions in the country and abroad.

arxiv:2512.13753.title: Time‐Aware UNet and Super‐Resolution Deep Residual Networks for Spatial Downscaling
arxiv:2512.13753.summary: Satellite observations of atmospheric pollutants are often available only at coarse spatial resolution, which limits their use in local‐scale environmental analysis. doi:10.1111/jfr3.70144.title: Comparative Evaluation of Deep Learning–Based Super–Resolution Models for Urban Flood Mapping
doi:10.1111/jfr3.70144.summary: Urban flood forecasting benefits from high‐resolution inundation maps, but fine‐grid hydrodynamic simulations are computationally costly. We compared three CNN–based super–resolution (SR) models, ResUNet, EDSR, and RCAN, for downscaling physics–based simulations in downtown Portland, Oregon, using paired flood maps at 1 m (HR) and both 4 and 8 m (LR). Performance was assessed using image level metrics (PSNR, SSIM) and flood specific indicators: CSI for flood extent, RMSE for water depth accuracy, and a depth–based severity classification. At 4× upscaling, all SR models outperformed the LR baseline; RCAN performed best (PSNR +57%, SSIM +31%, RMSE −73%, CSI +53%), followed by EDSR (PSNR +50%, SSIM +30%, RMSE −64%, CSI +45%) and ResUNet (RMSE −55%, CSI +40%). Analysis of class–wise recall showed RCAN leading for non–flood (98.06%, +6.59 pp) and severe flood (96.48%, +16.90 pp), while EDSR led for mild flood class (97.95%, +6.49 pp). Errors were most pronounced along wet–dry boundaries and in complex urban geometries, where RCAN and EDSR reduced error magnitude more effectively than ResUNet. Models with larger numbers of parameters required longer training times. Furthermore, the computational cost further increased with more training epochs and especially at 4× upscaling relative to 8×, reflecting differences in model complexity and scaling configuration. Taken together, these findings support SR as a practical complement to physics–based modeling for real time forecasting and planning, while also providing guidance for selecting architectures under varying computational budgets.

arxiv:2604.09505.summary: Super-resolution (SR) techniques based on deep learning have recently emerged as a promising approach to enhance the spatial resolution of computational fluid dynamics simulations while containing computational cost. doi:10.1002/joc.70287.summary: In the era of global warming, drought remains one of the most pressing, insidious and complex climatic phenomena. Although Global Climate Models (GCMs) are indispensable for simulating past and future climate patterns, they continue to face persistent challenges in accurately characterising drought under diverse climate conditions due to inherent model uncertainties. Multi‐model ensembles (MMEs) are widely adopted to reduce these uncertainties; however, conventional MME approaches often overlook three critical aspects: (i) the independent relative contribution of individual GCMs, (ii) the influence of point‐wise value deviations and (iii) the sequential order of predictor inclusion in the analysis. Neglecting these factors can result in biassed weighting, reduced interpretability and overestimation of drought severity in subsequent assessments. This study introduces an integrated two‐stage framework, Integrated Ensemble Based on Sequential Predictor Contribution Analysis for Standardised Climate Indices (IEBSPCASCI), for future drought assessment using GCM projections, combining a novel weighting strategy with an optimised drought index formulation. In Stage 1, we propose the sequential relative impact weighting ensemble (SRIWE), a new GCM ensemble weighting scheme that accounts for point‐wise discrepancies and sequential predictor contributions with addressing multicollinearity among models; in Stage 2, we develop the Standardised Partitioned Impact Severity Drought Index (SPISDI), an optimal‐standardisation‐based index enhancing drought severity quantification under future climate scenarios. The proposed IEBSPCASCI framework is applied to 94 locations in Pakistan using 22 GCM from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) for the period 1950–2014. The Stage 1 weighting scheme, SRIWE, outperforms conventional MMEs, achieving the highest median and mean Kling–Gupta Efficiency (KGE) (0.2650, 0.2435) and Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) (0.2074, 0.1075), and the lowest median and mean values of Mean Absolute Error (MAE) (12.5572, 18.027), indicating superior predictive skill and smaller errors. In stage 2, SPISDI‐based drought assessments reveal a consistent increase in drought severity and frequency in all SSP scenarios. Under SSP5‐8.5, the intensity of drought peaks markedly towards 2080–2100, signalling substantial climate‐induced risks to water resources and agriculture. Steady‐state probability analysis indicates that normal drought conditions dominate; however, extreme drought (ED) and severe drought (SD) events remain significant, with ED peaking at 2.37% (SSP2–4.5, 48 months) and SD reaching 8.6% (SSP1–2.6, 48 months). These findings underscore the urgent need for adaptive water management policies, climate‐resilient agricultural strategies and proactive drought risk governance to mitigate future socio‐economic impacts.

doi:10.24963/ijcai.2026/996.title: CrossRefine: A Microservice for Cross-Domain Spatial Super-Resolution
doi:10.24963/ijcai.2026/996.summary: High-resolution spatial fields are critical for local decision-making, yet many operational and scientific workflows produce coarse outputs due to computational limits. We present CrossRefine, a deployable microservice for cross-domain spatial super-resolution that enhances multi-channel spatial tiles without modifying upstream models. It is built around a unified, topography-conditioned adversarial UNet trained across geographically diverse regions to ensure robustness to heterogeneous terrains and domain shifts. Unlike region-specific enhancement models, the system generalizes across domains within a single architecture, balancing numerical fidelity and structural realism through a hybrid regression–adversarial objective. The service provides REST API endpoints for batch and streaming inference, supports mixed-precision, and offers per-tile diagnostics and confidence maps to promote safe deployment. In our demo, we show interactive refinement of coarse spatial inputs, side-by-side comparison with interpolation and non-adversarial baselines, and real-time profiling of latency and throughput on commodity hardware. CrossRefine illustrates how spatial super-resolution can be delivered as a practical AI microservice, enabling scalable refinement of existing computational workflows without requiring higher-resolution upstream simulations. doi:10.23919/date69613.2026.11539629.title: SuperPhys-Net: A Physics-Informed Super-Resolution Electromagnetic Simulator for Nanophotonic Devices
doi:10.23919/date69613.2026.11539629.summary: The rapid advancement of photonic integrated circuits is driving innovations in interconnect, computing, and sensing applications. This progress has led to the development of nanophotonic waveguide devices with complex geometries, offering greater design flexibility and a wider range of functional applications. However, electromagnetic (EM) simulation imposes a heavy computational burden during the design and validation phases. This significantly hampers design iteration speed and scalability. Although existing data-driven methods and physics-informed neural networks have shown promise for simpler structures, they fall short for highly complex geometries, limiting the automation of photonic device design. To address these issues, we present the SuperPhys-Net framework. This innovative approach enhances coarse-grid simulation results through super-resolution and integrates physical constraints to generate fine-grid solutions that adhere to physical laws. Our model demonstrates outstanding performance across complex nanophotonic waveguide devices with varying dimensions, achieving a 72.61% improvement in accuracy over current state-of-the-art models. Additionally, it reduces computational time by 76.09% compared to standard finite-difference frequency-domain solvers, all while maintaining exceptional accuracy across all scales.

doi:10.1109/icosec70158.2026.11735864.title: Dynamic Window Shifting Swin Transformer for Remote Sensing Scene Classification
doi:10.1109/icosec70158.2026.11735864.summary: Remote sensing scene classification is a difficult task because intra-class variability is high, background patterns are typically complex, and there is often substantial spatial-scale variation between aerial and satellite images. This paper proposes DWS-SwinT, a Dynamic Window Shifting Swin Transformer that augments the standard Swin Transformer with an adaptive window-displacement mechanism. In contrast to fixed-shift attention strategies, the proposed strategy dynamically computes window-shift offsets based on feature statistics, enabling a better model of spatial dependencies across scales while adding only slight computational overhead (+0.3 M parameters, +0.2 GFLOPs, and +0.2 ms inference time). Four benchmark datasets, including RSI-CB128, NWPU-RESISC45, UC Merced, and AID, were tested extensively. DWS-SwinT on the RSI-CB128 dataset achieved 98.88% classification accuracy, macro-AUC of 0.998, and cross-validated accuracy of 98.83% with a variance of 0.13, demonstrating strong performance compared to 11 state-of-the-art convolutional and transformer-based models, including MaxViT, InternImage, and DINOv2. Statistical significance $(\mathbf{p}<\mathbf{0. 0 0 1})$ was established using the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test, paired t-test, and Friedman-Nemenyi analysis. Moreover, robustness analysis in the presence of corrupt images with five corruption levels showed an improvement in performance of 1.85-2.67 percentage points compared to the Swin-B baseline. The observations of the attention-map visualizations also confirmed the success and comprehension of the suggested adaptive window-shifting approach. The findings reveal that DWS-SwinT is a robust, accurate, and computationally efficient remote sensing method for scene classification.

arxiv:2603.13584.title: An Empirical Investigation of Pre-Trained Deep Learning Model Reuse in the Scientific Process
arxiv:2603.13584.summary: Deep learning has achieved recognition for its impact within natural sciences, yet the prohibitive financial and technical cost of training models from scratch inhibits adoption. Following software engineering community guidance, natural scientists are reusing pre-trained deep learning models (PTMs) to amortize these costs. While prior works recommend PTM reuse patterns, we present the first empirical study of these patterns in the natural sciences, quantifying the utilization and impact of PTM reuse within the scientific process across 17,718 peer reviewed, open access papers. Our results show that “Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology” has outpaced other natural scientific fields in PTM reuse, “adaptation” reuse is the most prevalent PTM reuse pattern identified across all natural science fields, and the “testing” stage of the scientific process has been most impacted by PTM integration.

doi:10.1109/icicml67980.2025.11333444.title: CBCT-to-MRI Cross-Modality Translation using Cascaded Transfer Learning and Enhanced Generative Adversarial Networks
doi:10.1109/icicml67980.2025.11333444.summary: This study tackles the challenging CBCT-to-MRI translation by proposing a cascaded transfer learning (CTL) framework that decomposes the task into two stages: CBCT-to-CT (G1) and CT-to-MRI (G2). The generator is enhanced with multi-scale residuals and channel-spatial attention to recover soft tissue details, and is trained using a comprehensive loss function combining adversarial, L~1~, SSIM, perceptual, and gradient terms to ensure high fidelity. The final model leverages weights from the pre-trained G1 and G2 for initialization. Ablation studies confirm the superiority of our full method, which achieves significantly higher PSNR and SSIM than variants lacking either the cascade or the enhancement module.
